chapters.title: The Bow Hung Up
chapters.html:
Genesis 9

1And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.

2And the fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every living thing of the earth, and upon every bird of the heavens, upon everything that the ground creeps with, and upon all the fish of the sea. Into your hand they are given.

3Every creeping thing that is alive shall be food for you. Like the green plants, I have given you everything.

4But flesh with its soul — its blood — you shall not eat.

5And surely your blood, for your souls, I will require. From the hand of every living thing I will require it, and from the hand of the human — from the hand of a man's brother — I will require the soul of the human.

6One who sheds the blood of the human,
by the human shall his blood be shed,
for in the image of God He made the human.

7And you, be fruitful and multiply; swarm in the earth and multiply in it."

The Bow

8And God said to Noah and to his sons with him, saying,

9"And I — look, I am raising up My covenant with you, and with your seed after you,

10and with every living soul that is with you: in the bird, in the cattle, and in every living thing of the earth with you — from all that came out of the box, to every living thing of the earth.

11And I raise up My covenant with you: never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to ruin the earth."

12And God said, "This is the sign of the covenant that I am giving between Me and you and every living soul that is with you, for everlasting generations:

13My bow I have set in the cloud, and it shall be for a sign of covenant between Me and the earth.

14And it shall be, when I cloud a cloud over the earth, that the bow shall be seen in the cloud.

15And I will remember My covenant that is between Me and you and every living soul in all flesh, and never again shall the waters become a flood to ruin all flesh.

16And the bow shall be in the cloud, and I will see it, to remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living soul in all flesh that is upon the earth."

17And God said to Noah, "This is the sign of the covenant that I have raised up between Me and all flesh that is upon the earth."

The Vineyard

18And the sons of Noah who came out of the box were Shem and Ham and Japheth. And Ham, he is the father of Canaan.

19These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the whole earth was scattered.

20And Noah began — a man of the ground — and he planted a vineyard.

21And he drank from the wine and became drunk, and he uncovered himself inside his tent.

22And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father, and he told his two brothers outside.

23And Shem and Japheth took the garment and laid it on the shoulder of the two of them, and they walked backward and covered the nakedness of their father. And their faces were backward, and they did not see the nakedness of their father.

24And Noah woke from his wine, and he knew what his youngest son had done to him.

25And he said,
"Cursed be Canaan.
A servant of servants shall he be to his brothers."

26And he said,
"Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem,
and let Canaan be a servant to them.

27May God make wide for Japheth,
and let him dwell in the tents of Shem,
and let Canaan be a servant to them."

28And Noah lived after the flood three hundred and fifty years.

29And all the days of Noah were nine hundred and fifty years. And he died.

Notes

  • v1 "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth" — word for word from 1:28, the blessing on the first humans. But read what is not repeated: 1:28 continued and subdue it, and hold sway. Those two hard verbs, kavash and radah, are gone. What replaces them in v2 is fear and dread. The first humans were given rule; these are given terror. It is a colder arrangement, and the omission is the argument.

  • v3 "Every creeping thing that is alive shall be food for you" — in 1:29–30, both humans and animals were given plants. Eating meat is permitted here for the first time, and the sentence that grants it points straight back: like the green plants, I have given you everything.

  • v4 "flesh with its soul — its blood" — basar be-nafsho damo. The nephesh — the same word rendered "soul" throughout chapters 1 and 2, whose root sense is throat — is identified with the blood. The prohibition is not hygiene. It is that the life belongs to someone else, and you may have the animal but not that.

  • v5 "I will require" — edrosh, three times in one verse. The verb means to seek out, to inquire after, to go looking for. Blood is not merely avenged; it is sought, the way you search for something owed to you. The same picture as 4:10, where Abel's blood cried out from the ground.

  • v6 — set as lines because the Hebrew is a perfect mirror. Word by word: shofekh / dam / ha-adam / ba-adam / damo / yishaphekh — shedder, blood, the human, by the human, his blood, shall be shed. The sentence turns around at its middle and walks back out the way it came in, so the punishment is the crime reversed, in the shape of the line itself. No English word order can reproduce it; the lineation is an attempt to let the turn be felt.

  • v6 "by the human" — ba-adam, which can be "by a human," "in the human," or "for the human." The preposition is doing real work and is not decidable here. Whether this verse establishes human courts or states a principle about God's own requiring depends on which sense is chosen, and the Hebrew does not choose.

  • v6 "in the image of God" — be-tselem Elohim, quoting 1:27. The reason murder is intolerable is not the value of life in general; it is that the thing destroyed was a likeness.

  • v13 "My bow" — qashti. This is not a word for a rainbow. Qeshet is the war bow, the weapon — it is the word used when a soldier draws a bow throughout the Hebrew Bible, and Hebrew has no separate term for the arc in the sky. So the sentence is: My weapon I have set in the cloud. A bow hung in the clouds is a bow that has been put down, and one hung with its curve upward is a bow pointed away from the earth. English "rainbow" turns a laid-down weapon into a weather phenomenon.

  • v14 "when I cloud a cloud" — be-'anni 'anan, the verb and its noun from one root, the way Hebrew likes to do it. Kept literal because the smoothing to "when I bring clouds" loses the doubling.

  • vv15–16 "I will remember… to remember" — zakhar again, the verb from 8:1 where God remembered Noah. The sign in the sky is not for the humans to see and take comfort; both verses say it is so that God will see it and remember. The covenant's reminder points upward.

  • v20 "a man of the ground" — ish ha-adamah. Cain in 4:2 was an oved adamah, a worker of the ground. Noah, who was named for relief from the ground's curse in 5:29, becomes a man of the ground — and the first thing the restarted world produces is a drunk man naked in a tent.

  • v21 "he uncovered himself" — va-yitgal, reflexive: he uncovered himself. Not "was uncovered." What follows is his own doing first.

  • v22, 23 "nakedness" — 'ervah. The word covers ordinary nakedness and also functions in legal contexts as a term for sexual transgression, which is why v24's "what his youngest son had done to him" has been read as more than looking. The Hebrew says saw and then says done. Both words are there, and the gap between them is not filled in.

  • v25 "Cursed be Canaan" — Ham commits the act; Canaan, Ham's son, who has not appeared in the scene, receives the curse. The text states this without explaining it, and v18 and v22 both go out of their way to remind the reader whose father Ham is. Reported as it stands.

  • v27 "May God make wide for Japheth" — yapht Elohim le-Yephet, a pun: the verb yapht (make wide, make room) chimes with the name Yephet. Like Noah's own name in 5:29, the blessing is built out of the sound of the name rather than its derivation.

chapters.title: The Nations, by Their Tongues
chapters.html:
Genesis 10

1And these are the begettings of the sons of Noah — Shem, Ham, and Japheth — and sons were born to them after the flood.

Japheth

2The sons of Japheth: Gomer and Magog and Madai and Javan and Tubal and Meshech and Tiras.

3And the sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz and Riphath and Togarmah.

4And the sons of Javan: Elishah and Tarshish, Kittim and Dodanim.

5From these the coastlands of the nations separated out in their lands, each by his tongue, by their families, in their nations.

Ham

6And the sons of Ham: Cush and Egypt and Put and Canaan.

7And the sons of Cush: Seba and Havilah and Sabtah and Raamah and Sabteca. And the sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.

8And Cush fathered Nimrod. He began to be a mighty one in the earth.

9He was a mighty hunter before the LORD. Therefore it is said, "Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the LORD."

10And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel and Erech and Akkad and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.

11From that land went out Asshur, and he built Nineveh and Rehoboth-Ir and Calah,

12and Resen between Nineveh and Calah — that is the great city.

13And Egypt fathered the Ludim and the Anamim and the Lehabim and the Naphtuhim,

14and the Pathrusim and the Casluhim — from whom the Philistines went out — and the Caphtorim.

15And Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn, and Heth,

16and the Jebusite and the Amorite and the Girgashite,

17and the Hivite and the Arkite and the Sinite,

18and the Arvadite and the Zemarite and the Hamathite. And afterward the families of the Canaanite were scattered.

19And the border of the Canaanite was from Sidon, as you come toward Gerar, as far as Gaza; as you come toward Sodom and Gomorrah and Admah and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.

20These are the sons of Ham, by their families, by their tongues, in their lands, in their nations.

Shem

21And to Shem, to him also, children were born — the father of all the sons of Eber, the brother of Japheth the elder.

22The sons of Shem: Elam and Asshur and Arpachshad and Lud and Aram.

23And the sons of Aram: Uz and Hul and Gether and Mash.

24And Arpachshad fathered Shelah, and Shelah fathered Eber.

25And to Eber were born two sons. The name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided; and the name of his brother was Joktan.

26And Joktan fathered Almodad and Sheleph and Hazarmaveth and Jerah,

27and Hadoram and Uzal and Diklah,

28and Obal and Abimael and Sheba,

29and Ophir and Havilah and Jobab. All these were the sons of Joktan.

30And their dwelling was from Mesha, as you come toward Sephar, the mountain of the east.

31These are the sons of Shem, by their families, by their tongues, in their lands, by their nations.

32These are the families of the sons of Noah, by their begettings, in their nations. And from these the nations separated out in the earth after the flood.

Notes

  • vv5, 20, 31 "by their tongues" — li-lshonotam, three times, once at the close of each branch. The nations here already have separate languages, and they already have separate lands. The next chapter opens with the whole earth speaking one lip and one set of words, and ends with languages being divided at Babel. The two chapters do not run in sequence. Chapter 10 is the outcome; chapter 11 goes back and tells how it happened. Hebrew narrative does this often — finish a line, then step back — and English readers who expect chapters to follow one another in time find a contradiction where the text intends an overlap.

  • v5 "separated out" — niphredu, and the same verb closes the chapter in v32. The word for what happens to the nations is separation, the neutral term you would use of branches dividing. Nothing here is a punishment yet.

  • v8 "He began" — hechel. This verb has been quietly marking the chapter turns: then it was begun to call on the name of the LORD (4:26), humankind began to be many (6:1), Noah began as a man of the ground (9:20), and now Nimrod begins to be a mighty one. Four beginnings, and the last two go badly.

  • v8, 9 "a mighty one… a mighty hunter" — gibbor, the same word as ha-gibborim in 6:4, the mighty ones born before the flood who were "the men of the name." The flood was supposed to have ended them. Four verses after the last genealogy, the word is back.

  • v9 "before the LORD" — lifnei YHWH, which ordinarily means in the presence of and carries no criticism at all. Every sinister reading of Nimrod — hunter of men, rebel, tyrant — comes from later tradition, not from these two verses. What the Hebrew says is that he was famous enough to become a proverb, and that his kingdom began at Babel.

  • v10 "Babel" — named here, in the land of Shinar, before chapter 11 gets to it. The reader is told whose city it is before being told what happened there.

  • v11 "From that land went out Asshur" — the Hebrew can equally be read from that land he went out to Asshur, with Nimrod as the subject continuing from v10. Asshur is both a personal name and the land of Assyria, and nothing in the grammar decides it. The choice changes who founded Nineveh.

  • v21 "the brother of Japheth the elder" — achi Yephet ha-gadol. The adjective sits at the end and can attach to either brother: Shem, the elder brother of Japheth, or the brother of Japheth the elder. English translations split on it, usually silently. The Hebrew is genuinely ambiguous about which of Noah's sons was the firstborn.

  • v25 "Peleg" — the verse explains the name in the same breath: for in his days the earth was divided, niphlegah, from the root palag. Name and reason are the same word in Hebrew and unrelated sounds in English. Note also that palag is not the parad of vv5 and 32 — a different word for a different dividing, and the text does not say which one it has in mind.

  • The shape — Japheth gets four verses, Ham gets fifteen, Shem gets eleven. The branch that matters least to the rest of the book is dealt with first and fastest; the line the book will follow is saved for last. That ordering — youngest or least first, chosen last — is how this book introduces nearly everyone.

chapters.title: One Lip, and the Scattering
chapters.html:
Genesis 11

1And all the earth was one lip and one set of words.

2And it came to pass, as they journeyed from the east, that they found a valley in the land of Shinar, and they settled there.

3And they said, each to his neighbor, "Come, let us brick bricks, and burn them to a burning." And the brick was stone to them, and the bitumen was mortar to them.

4And they said, "Come, let us build for ourselves a city, and a tower with its head in the heavens. And let us make for ourselves a name, lest we be scattered over the face of all the earth."

5And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower that the sons of man had built.

6And the LORD said, "Look — one people, and one lip for all of them, and this is what they begin to do. And now nothing will be held back from them, all that they scheme to do.

7Come, let us go down, and let us confuse their lip there, so that they will not hear, each the lip of his neighbor."

8And the LORD scattered them from there over the face of all the earth, and they left off building the city.

9Therefore its name was called Babel, for there the LORD confused the lip of all the earth, and from there the LORD scattered them over the face of all the earth.

The Begettings of Shem

10These are the begettings of Shem. Shem was a hundred years old, and he fathered Arpachshad, two years after the flood.

11And Shem lived after he fathered Arpachshad five hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

12And Arpachshad lived thirty-five years, and he fathered Shelah.

13And Arpachshad lived after he fathered Shelah four hundred and three years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

14And Shelah lived thirty years, and he fathered Eber.

15And Shelah lived after he fathered Eber four hundred and three years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

16And Eber lived thirty-four years, and he fathered Peleg.

17And Eber lived after he fathered Peleg four hundred and thirty years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

18And Peleg lived thirty years, and he fathered Reu.

19And Peleg lived after he fathered Reu two hundred and nine years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

20And Reu lived thirty-two years, and he fathered Serug.

21And Reu lived after he fathered Serug two hundred and seven years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

22And Serug lived thirty years, and he fathered Nahor.

23And Serug lived after he fathered Nahor two hundred years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

24And Nahor lived twenty-nine years, and he fathered Terah.

25And Nahor lived after he fathered Terah a hundred and nineteen years, and he fathered sons and daughters.

26And Terah lived seventy years, and he fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

The Begettings of Terah

27And these are the begettings of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and Haran fathered Lot.

28And Haran died before the face of Terah his father, in the land of his kindred, in Ur of the Chaldeans.

29And Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves. The name of Abram's wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor's wife was Milcah, daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah and the father of Iscah.

30And Sarai was barren. She had no child.

31And Terah took Abram his son, and Lot son of Haran, his son's son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of Abram his son, and they went out with them from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan. And they came as far as Harran, and they settled there.

32And the days of Terah were two hundred and five years, and Terah died in Harran.

Notes

  • v1 "one lip and one set of words" — saphah echat u-devarim achadim. Saphah is the lip, the body part; Hebrew names a language by the thing it is spoken with. English "language" comes from Latin lingua, the tongue, so we do the same and have stopped hearing it. Kept literal throughout this chapter because the word recurs five times and the story is about mouths.

  • v3 "let us brick bricks, and burn them to a burning" — nilbenah levenim… ve-nisrephah li-srephah. Twice the verb takes its own noun as its object, which is a construction Hebrew uses for emphasis and which English can only imitate clumsily. The clumsiness is the point: the sentence is people talking themselves into work. And then the same line puns twice more — ha-levenah le-aven, the brick became their stone, and ha-chemar… la-chomer, the bitumen their mortar. Four sound-pairs in one verse. The building project is made of wordplay before it is made of brick.

  • v4 "let us make for ourselves a name" — na'aseh lanu shem. This phrase has a history in the book. In 6:4 the mighty ones before the flood were anshei ha-shem, the men of the name. Here men decide to make one for themselves. And at the top of the very next chapter, God says to Abram I will make your name great — the same thing, given rather than seized, three verses after this story ends. The tower and the call are set side by side on purpose.

  • v4 "lest we be scattered" — pen naphuts. In v8, va-yaphets YHWH otam, the LORD scattered them. The thing they build the tower to prevent is exactly what happens, and the text uses the same root for the fear and the outcome.

  • v5 "the LORD came down to see" — the tower's head is in the heavens, and God has to come down to look at it. Nothing in the verse mocks them; it simply reports the descent, and lets the distance speak.

  • v7 "Come, let us go down" — havah neredah, answering their havah nilbenah (v3) and havah nivneh (v4). Three times someone says havah, "come now" — twice by the builders, once from above. The reply is in their own words.

  • v7 "so that they will not hear" — asher lo yishme'u, hear. Not "understand." The confusion is at the level of sound: the noise still arrives, and nothing comes of it.

  • v9 "Babel… confused" — Babel… balal. In Akkadian, the language of the city itself, Bab-ilu means gate of god, and that is what its own people understood the name to mean. Hebrew hears something else in it — balal, to mix, to confound — and the verse builds the whole naming on that hearing. It is not an etymology; it is a rival one.

  • vv10–26 "and he fathered sons and daughters" — compare chapter 5, where the identical formula ran with one addition: and he died, eight times, like a drum. Here that clause is gone. Nine generations pass and the text does not say that any of them died. The first death recorded after the flood is Haran's in v28, and the first completed lifespan is Terah's in v32, the last verse before Abram is called.

  • The numbers — Shem lives 600 years all told; by Peleg it is 239, by Nahor 148, by Terah 205. The lifespans are collapsing across the chapter, and the collapse lands exactly where the story stops being about the world and starts being about one family.

  • v28 "died before the face of Terah his father" — al penei Terach aviv. The first time in the Bible a son dies while his father watches. It is stated in eight words and not commented on.

  • v30 "And Sarai was barren. She had no child." — two short clauses saying the same thing twice, which Hebrew narrative almost never does without reason. Everything that follows for the next ten chapters is this sentence.

  • v31 "Harran" — a different word from Haran the son in v27. The man is spelled with an initial he; the town is spelled with an initial chet. They are unrelated words that English collapses into one spelling, so an English reader sees Terah's dead son's name on the town where Terah stops and dies, and hears a resonance that is not in the Hebrew.

  • v31 "to go to the land of Canaan. And they came as far as Harran, and they settled there." — Terah sets out for Canaan and does not arrive. The journey Abram is called to make in 12:1 was already begun by his father, and abandoned halfway.

chapters.title: Go, For Yourself
chapters.html:
Genesis 12

1And the LORD said to Abram, "Go, for yourself, from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you.

2And I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will make your name great. And be a blessing.

3And I will bless those who bless you, and the one who treats you lightly I will curse. And in you all the families of the ground shall be blessed."

4And Abram went, as the LORD had spoken to him, and Lot went with him. And Abram was seventy-five years old when he went out from Harran.

5And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all their possessions that they had gathered, and the souls they had made in Harran, and they went out to go to the land of Canaan. And they came to the land of Canaan.

6And Abram passed through the land as far as the place of Shechem, as far as the oak of Moreh. And the Canaanite was then in the land.

7And the LORD appeared to Abram and said, "To your seed I will give this land." And he built there an altar to the LORD who had appeared to him.

8And he moved on from there to the hill country east of Bethel, and he pitched his tent — Bethel on the west and Ai on the east. And he built there an altar to the LORD, and he called on the name of the LORD.

9And Abram journeyed, going and journeying, toward the Negev.

Down to Egypt

10And there was a famine in the land, and Abram went down to Egypt to sojourn there, for the famine was heavy in the land.

11And it came to pass, as he drew near to come into Egypt, that he said to Sarai his wife, "Look now — I know that you are a woman beautiful to look at.

12And it will be, when the Egyptians see you, that they will say, 'This is his wife,' and they will kill me, and you they will keep alive.

13Say, please, that you are my sister, so that it may go well with me on your account, and my soul may live because of you."

14And it came to pass, when Abram came into Egypt, that the Egyptians saw the woman, that she was very beautiful.

15And the officials of Pharaoh saw her, and they praised her to Pharaoh, and the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house.

16And he dealt well with Abram on her account, and he had flocks and cattle and donkeys and male servants and female servants and she-donkeys and camels.

17And the LORD struck Pharaoh with great strikes, and his house also, over the matter of Sarai, Abram's wife.

18And Pharaoh called Abram and said, "What is this you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife?

19Why did you say, 'She is my sister,' so that I took her for myself as a wife? And now — here is your wife. Take her and go."

20And Pharaoh gave men orders concerning him, and they sent him away, and his wife, and all that was his.

Notes

  • v1 "Go, for yourself" — lekh lekha, two words, and the second one has defeated every translator. It is the verb go followed by a preposition meaning to you or for you — a construction Hebrew uses to throw the action back on the one doing it. "Go by yourself," "go for your own sake," "get yourself gone," "go, you." Most English Bibles print "Go" and drop the second word entirely. Something is being said to Abram about himself in the command, and it cannot be carried over.

  • v1 "from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father's house" — three phrases, and they narrow. Country, then clan, then the household you sleep in. If they ran the other way it would be a list; running this way it is a tightening, each step costing more than the one before, ending on the smallest and hardest thing to leave.

  • v1 "the land that I will show you" — asher ar'ekka. He is not told where. The destination is withheld in the same sentence that commands the departure, and the verb is future: that I will show you, not that I have shown you.

  • vv2–3 "bless" — the root barakh five times in two verses, after the previous eleven chapters have handed out curse after curse — the serpent, the ground, Cain, Canaan. The word turns over here and stays turned for the rest of the book.

  • v2 "I will make your name great" — va-agaddelah shemekha. Eight verses earlier, the builders at Babel said let us make for ourselves a name — na'aseh lanu shem. Same noun, opposite direction. They seized; he is given. The two stories are placed back to back so that the second answers the first, and an English reader who cannot see shem in both sentences will never notice the reply.

  • v2 "And be a blessing" — ve-heyeh berakhah, an imperative. Not "you will be blessed" but a command to be one. It sits at the end of a list of things God will do, and hands one back.

  • v3 "the one who treats you lightly" — u-meqallelkha, from qalal, whose root sense is to be light, slight, of no weight. Hebrew has a heavier word for cursing, arar, and it uses that one in the very next clause for what God will do. So the sentence is not symmetrical: those who make you light I will curse. English prints "curse" twice and loses the imbalance.

  • v3 "in you all the families of the ground shall be blessed" — ve-nivrekhu vekha. The verb form can be passive (shall be blessed) or reflexive (shall bless themselves by you — that is, shall use your name when they pronounce a blessing). Both are grammatically available and the difference is large. Also note it is families of the ground, adamah, not "of the earth" — the ground that was cursed in 3:17 because of the man.

  • v5 "the souls they had made in Harran" — ha-nephesh asher asu be-Charan. An odd phrase. Nephesh is the throat-word rendered "living soul" throughout chapters 1–2; asu is simply "made." People they acquired, or people they somehow made. The Hebrew does not explain itself, and translations that print "the people they had acquired" are choosing.

  • v6 "And the Canaanite was then in the land" — the narrator stepping outside the story to tell the reader something about the time it happened. The word is az, then — which implies a now when it is no longer so.

  • vv10–20 — read the sequence and then read the book of Exodus: a famine drives the family down to Egypt; the Egyptian ruler takes what is not his; the LORD strikes Pharaoh with nega'im, great strikes or plagues; and Pharaoh sends them away — va-yeshallechu, the verb Moses will use again and again — with livestock, silver and servants they did not have when they came. The whole Exodus is in these eleven verses, in miniature, four hundred years early.

  • v13 "so that it may go well with me on your account, and my soul may live because of you" — two clauses, both about him, both ending in you. He is asking her to carry the risk and states the benefit twice, in his own name.

  • vv14–16 — Sarai does not speak. She is seen, praised, taken, and Abram is paid, and she says nothing in any of it. Neither does he.

chapters.title: Lot Lifted His Eyes
chapters.html:
Genesis 13

1And Abram went up from Egypt — he and his wife and all that was his, and Lot with him — toward the Negev.

2And Abram was very heavy in livestock, in silver, and in gold.

3And he went on his journeys from the Negev as far as Bethel, to the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and Ai,

4to the place of the altar that he had made there at the first. And Abram called there on the name of the LORD.

5And Lot also, who went with Abram, had flocks and cattle and tents.

6And the land could not carry them, to settle together, for their possessions were many, and they were not able to settle together.

7And there was quarreling between the herdsmen of Abram's livestock and the herdsmen of Lot's livestock. And the Canaanite and the Perizzite were then settled in the land.

The Choice

8And Abram said to Lot, "Let there not be quarreling, please, between me and you, and between my herdsmen and your herdsmen, for we are men, brothers.

9Is not all the land before you? Separate, please, from me. If to the left, then I will go right; and if to the right, then I will go left."

10And Lot lifted his eyes and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that all of it was well watered — before the LORD ruined Sodom and Gomorrah — like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, as you come toward Zoar.

11And Lot chose for himself all the plain of the Jordan, and Lot journeyed eastward, and they separated, each from his brother.

12Abram settled in the land of Canaan, and Lot settled in the cities of the plain, and he pitched his tent as far as Sodom.

13And the men of Sodom were evil, and sinners against the LORD, exceedingly.

Lift Your Eyes

14And the LORD said to Abram, after Lot had separated from him, "Lift up, please, your eyes, and look from the place where you are — northward and southward and eastward and seaward.

15For all the land that you see, to you I will give it, and to your seed, forever.

16And I will make your seed like the dust of the earth, so that if a man could count the dust of the earth, then your seed also could be counted.

17Rise, walk about in the land, through its length and through its breadth, for to you I will give it."

18And Abram moved his tent, and he came and settled by the oaks of Mamre, which are in Hebron. And he built there an altar to the LORD.

Notes

  • v2 "very heavy" — kaved me'od. Three verses earlier, in 12:10, the reason he went down to Egypt was that the famine was kaved, heavy, in the land. He goes down because of heaviness and comes back up heavy. The same word does both jobs, and the second is the wages of the lie he told in between — the livestock and servants of 12:16, given to him for his wife.

  • v6 "the land could not carry them" — lo nasa otam ha-arets, the land did not lift or bear them. The same verb, nasa, that Lot uses four verses later when he lifts his eyes, and that God uses to Abram in v14. The land could not lift them; so they lift their eyes instead, and are divided by what they see.

  • v8 "we are men, brothers" — anashim achim anachnu. Lot is Abram's nephew, not his brother; ach in Hebrew covers the whole range of male kin. But the word choice matters here, because v11 ends and they separated, each from his brother — and the last two brothers in this book to be alone in a field together were Cain and Abel. Abram proposes the opposite ending, and pays for it with first choice.

  • v9 "Separate, please, from me" — hippared na me-alai, from the root parad. It is the verb that ran through the table of nations in chapter 10: from these the nations separated out. What happened to the whole world in a genealogy happens here between two men over grazing.

  • v9 "If to the left, then I will go right" — Abram, who was promised this land in 12:7, gives it away with a coin-flip. He is the elder and holds the promise, and he offers the choice to the younger man with nothing.

  • v10 "Lot lifted his eyes and saw" — the chapter turns on two liftings of eyes. Lot lifts his own, and chooses. In v14 God tells Abram lift up your eyes — after the choosing is over, and what Abram sees is given rather than taken. The identical gesture, once seized and once received, three verses apart.

  • v10 "like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt" — two comparisons, and they do not sit comfortably together. One is Eden. The other is the country they have just been thrown out of. The narrator hands the reader both and does not choose between them.

  • v10 "before the LORD ruined Sodom and Gomorrah" — shachet, the verb that ran four times through 6:11–13, where the earth was ruined and God said I am ruining them. The word for the flood is attached to Sodom here, thirteen verses before Lot moves his tent there, and five chapters before it happens.

  • v11 "journeyed eastward" — mi-qedem, which is either from the east or eastward; the Hebrew is not decisive. But eastward is the direction of departure in this book. Cain went out east of Eden (4:16); the builders came from the east to Shinar (11:2); the cherubim were stationed east of the garden (3:24). Moving east is how people in Genesis leave.

  • v13 "the men of Sodom were evil, and sinners against the LORD, exceedingly" — ra'im ve-chatta'im… me'od. The narrator says this immediately after Lot pitches toward Sodom, so the reader knows what Lot does not. And me'od, exceedingly, is the word from 1:31 — everything God had made was tov me'od. The intensifier is the same; the noun it modifies has changed.

  • v14 "northward and southward and eastward and seaward" — the Hebrew for west is yammah, seaward, because the Mediterranean is what lies west of anyone standing in Canaan. The compass in this language is drawn from a body standing in one place: ahead is east, behind is west, the sea is the sunset.

  • v16 "like the dust of the earth" — ka-aphar ha-arets. Aphar is the dust the human was shaped from in 2:7 and returns to in 3:19. The promise of descendants is made in the word for what a body is made of and comes apart into.

  • v18 "the oaks of Mamre" — elonei, large trees; the word is related to el, and such trees mark sacred places all through the book. Abram has now built altars at Shechem (12:7), at Bethel (12:8), and here. He owns none of the land and has marked three points on it.

chapters.title: The Four Kings, and the Priest of Salem
chapters.html:
Genesis 14

1And it came to pass in the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim,

2that they made war with Bera king of Sodom, and with Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, and Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela — that is Zoar.

3All these joined together at the Valley of Siddim — that is the Salt Sea.

4Twelve years they had served Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled.

5And in the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer came, and the kings who were with him, and they struck the Rephaim in Ashteroth-karnaim, and the Zuzim in Ham, and the Emim in Shaveh-kiriathaim,

6and the Horite in their hill country of Seir, as far as El-paran, which is by the wilderness.

7And they turned back and came to En-mishpat — that is Kadesh — and they struck all the field of the Amalekite, and also the Amorite who was settled in Hazazon-tamar.

8And the king of Sodom went out, and the king of Gomorrah, and the king of Admah, and the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela — that is Zoar — and they set the battle in order against them in the Valley of Siddim:

9against Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar — four kings against the five.

10And the Valley of Siddim was pits upon pits of bitumen, and the king of Sodom and Gomorrah fled and fell in there, and those who remained fled to the hill country.

11And they took all the possessions of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their food, and they went.

12And they took Lot, the son of Abram's brother, and his possessions, and they went. And he was settled in Sodom.

The Man from Across

13And the escaped one came and told Abram the Hebrew — and he was dwelling by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner, and they were masters of a covenant with Abram.

14And Abram heard that his brother had been taken captive, and he emptied out his trained men, born of his house, three hundred and eighteen, and he pursued as far as Dan.

15And he divided himself against them by night — he and his servants — and struck them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, which is to the left of Damascus.

16And he brought back all the possessions, and also Lot his brother and his possessions he brought back, and also the women and the people.

Bread and Wine

17And the king of Sodom went out to meet him, after his return from striking Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, to the Valley of Shaveh — that is the King's Valley.

18And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. And he was a priest to God Most High.

19And he blessed him and said,
"Blessed be Abram to God Most High,
getter of heaven and earth.

20And blessed be God Most High,
who has delivered your foes into your hand."

And he gave him a tenth of everything.

21And the king of Sodom said to Abram, "Give me the souls, and the possessions take for yourself."

22And Abram said to the king of Sodom, "I have lifted my hand to the LORD, God Most High, getter of heaven and earth:

23not from a thread to a sandal-strap — I will not take from anything that is yours — so that you will not say, 'I made Abram rich.'

24Nothing for me. Only what the young men have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me: Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre — they shall take their share."

Notes

  • v2 "Bera… Birsha" — the first two names read, letter for letter, like be-ra, "in evil," and bi-rsha, "in wickedness." Whether these were their actual names, a scribal joke, or ordinary names that happen to sound that way is not something the text says or that anyone can establish. The resemblance is there in the consonants; the intent is not recoverable.

  • v10 "pits upon pits of bitumen" — be'erot be'erot chemar, the noun doubled, which is how Hebrew says full of them. And chemar is the same bitumen the builders used for mortar at Babel in 11:3. The stuff that held the tower together is what the kings of Sodom fall into.

  • v13 "Abram the Hebrew" — ha-Ivri, the first time in the Bible anyone is called this, and it is a foreigner's word for him — it appears when outsiders are looking. The word is built on ever, the far side, the region across: someone from the other side of the river. It is also the name of Shem's descendant Eber in 10:24 and 11:14. Whether the label comes from the ancestor or from the crossing, the sense is the same both ways. He is the man from across.

  • v13 "masters of a covenant with Abram" — ba'alei verit Avram. The first occurrence of berit, covenant, in the book is not between God and anyone — it is a treaty between Abram and three Amorite brothers. The word that will carry the rest of the Bible starts as ordinary politics between neighbors.

  • v14 "he emptied out his trained men" — va-yareq, from the root for emptying. He empties the household out like a container turned over. The word for the men, chanikhav, appears nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible; "trained" is a guess from a related root, and a good one, but a guess.

  • v18 "Melchizedek king of Salem" — Malki-tsedeq melekh Shalem. The name is two ordinary words, my king and righteousness, and the city is Shalem — which is also the ordinary word for whole, sound, at peace, the root behind shalom. A reader of the Hebrew hears titles where an English reader hears two proper nouns. He appears in three verses, blesses, is given a tenth, and is never mentioned again in this book.

  • v18 "a priest to God Most High" — kohen le-El Elyon. A priest, before there is any priesthood, of a God named with a title Abram has not used, in a city not his own. Nothing is explained. He is simply there, and Abram accepts his blessing and pays him.

  • v19, 22 "getter of heaven and earth" — qoneh shamayim va-arets. Qanah is the verb for acquiring, getting, taking possession — the same verb Eve used in 4:1 when she said qaniti ish, I have gotten a man. English usually prints "maker" or "creator" here, which is smoother and imports a different verb; Hebrew has bara and asah for that and does not use them. Note also what Abram does with the phrase in v22: he repeats Melchizedek's exact title and puts YHWH in front of it. He accepts the description and names who it belongs to.

  • v20 "who has delivered" — miggen, an unusual verb, related to magen, a shield. It means to hand over, but the shield is audible inside it — which matters, because the first words God says to Abram in the very next chapter are I am your shield, magen. The blessing and the answer share a root across the chapter break.

  • v20 "And he gave him a tenth of everything" — the Hebrew names neither man. And he gave him — Abram to Melchizedek, or Melchizedek to Abram. Word order and the flow of the scene favor Abram as the giver, and that is how it is almost always read, but the verse does not say so.

  • v21 "Give me the souls" — ten li ha-nephesh. The king of Sodom asks for the people and offers the goods. He uses the word nephesh, the throat-word for a living thing, of human beings who are being counted as recoverable property.

  • v23 "not from a thread to a sandal-strap" — mi-chut ve-ad serokh na'al. The smallest things a person could be given. The sentence in Hebrew is an unfinished oath: if from a thread… if I take… — the consequence is left off, which is how Hebrew swears. Saying the punishment aloud was avoided; the silence is the force of it.

  • v23 "so that you will not say, 'I made Abram rich'" — he has just been made rich once already, in Egypt, by a king who was paying for his wife (12:16). He does not let it happen twice.

chapters.title: The Cutting
chapters.html:
Genesis 15

1After these things the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision, saying, "Do not fear, Abram. I am a shield to you. Your reward is very great."

2And Abram said, "Lord GOD, what will You give me, and I am going stripped? And the son of the possession of my house — he is Eliezer of Damascus."

3And Abram said, "Look — to me You have given no seed, and here, a son of my house is inheriting me."

4And here, the word of the LORD came to him, saying, "This one shall not inherit you. Rather, one who comes out of your own inward parts — he shall inherit you."

5And He brought him outside and said, "Look now toward the heavens and count the stars, if you are able to count them." And He said to him, "So shall your seed be."

6And he trusted in the LORD, and He reckoned it to him as righteousness.

7And He said to him, "I am the LORD, who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to inherit it."

8And he said, "Lord GOD, by what shall I know that I will inherit it?"

Between the Pieces

9And He said to him, "Take for Me a heifer of three, and a she-goat of three, and a ram of three, and a turtledove, and a young pigeon."

10And he took for Him all of these, and he cut them in two through the middle, and he set each piece opposite its fellow. But the bird he did not cut.

11And the birds of prey came down upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them back.

12And it came to pass, as the sun was going down, that a deep sleep fell upon Abram; and here — a dread, a darkness, a great one, falling upon him.

13And He said to Abram, "Know, you must know, that your seed will be a sojourner in a land not theirs, and they will serve them, and they will afflict them, four hundred years.

14And also the nation that they serve, I am judging. And after that they will come out with great possessions.

15And you — you will come to your fathers in peace. You will be buried at a good gray age.

16And a fourth generation will return here, for the guilt of the Amorite is not yet complete."

17And it came to pass — the sun had gone down, and it was thick darkness — and here: a smoking oven and a torch of fire, which passed between those pieces.

18On that day the LORD cut a covenant with Abram, saying, "To your seed I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates:

19the Kenite, and the Kenizzite, and the Kadmonite,

20and the Hittite, and the Perizzite, and the Rephaim,

21and the Amorite, and the Canaanite, and the Girgashite, and the Jebusite."

Notes

  • v1 "I am a shield to you" — anokhi magen lakh. In 14:20 Melchizedek blessed God as the one who miggen — delivered — Abram's foes into his hand, a verb built on this same noun. The first words God speaks after that scene pick the word up and make it a title: not the one who shields you from something, but I am the shield.

  • v1 "Your reward is very great" — the Hebrew can also be read as a single clause with the preceding one: I am your shield, your very great reward. Both parsings are available and English Bibles divide on it.

  • v2 "I am going stripped" — ariri, a rare word for childless, with the sense of being stripped bare or left exposed. Not the ordinary term for having no children. He is describing a condition, not a statistic.

  • v2 "the son of the possession of my house — he is Eliezer of Damascus" — u-ven meshek beiti hu Dammeseq Eliezer. This is one of the genuinely obscure sentences in Genesis. Meshek occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible and nobody knows what it means; it resembles the name Dammeseq, Damascus, in a way that may be wordplay or may be coincidence. Every English version here is a reconstruction. Rendered word by word, opacity included, rather than smoothed into a sentence the Hebrew does not have.

  • v5 "count the stars" — in 13:16 the promise was like the dust of the earth, a thing you look down at and walk on. Here he is taken outside at night and told to look up. Same promise, two chapters apart, aimed in opposite directions — and the dust is what a body is made of, while the stars are what he is told he cannot number.

  • v6 "he trusted" — he'emin, from the root aman, which means to be firm, steady, reliable. The word amen comes from it. It is not primarily an assertion about facts; it is leaning your weight on something and finding it holds.

  • v6 "He reckoned it to him as righteousness" — va-yachshevehah lo tsedaqah. Chashav is an accounting verb: to count something into a column, to enter it in a reckoning. The sentence does not name either party — and he reckoned it to him — though the flow makes God the one doing the reckoning. What is striking in Hebrew is how commercial the verb is. Something is being credited to an account.

  • v9 "a heifer of three" — meshulleshet, from the number three. It may mean three years old, or it may mean three of each. The word is a form built on the number and does not specify. Left as "of three."

  • v10 "he cut them in two… but the bird he did not cut" — batar, to cut in pieces. Abram is not told what to do with the animals in v9; he is only told to take them. He cuts them himself, without instruction, because he knows what this is for.

  • v11 "Abram drove them back" — the one action he performs in the entire ceremony, and it is chasing scavengers off the meat while nothing happens. Then the sun goes down.

  • v12 "a deep sleep" — tardemah, the same word used in 2:21 when God put the man under to build the woman. It occurs rarely, and both times something is done to a sleeping man that he cannot participate in.

  • v12 "a dread, a darkness, a great one" — three words in apposition, eimah chashekhah gedolah, stacked without conjunctions. English wants "a great and dreadful darkness"; the Hebrew lays them side by side and lets them accumulate.

  • v17 "a smoking oven and a torch of fire, which passed between those pieces" — this is the point of the chapter, and it depends on knowing what cutting animals in half was for. Two parties to an oath walked between the pieces together, and the meaning was: let this be done to me if I break it. Here only one party walks. Abram is asleep, held down by darkness, and God passes through alone. The covenant is made with nobody on the other side of it.

  • v18 "cut a covenant" — karat berit, the standing Hebrew idiom for making an agreement: you cut a covenant. The metaphor is dead in ordinary usage, the way English "strike a bargain" is dead. This chapter wakes it up — the animals really are cut, the pieces really are laid out — and then uses the idiom in the summary verse, so the phrase lands on its literal sense.

  • v16 "the guilt of the Amorite is not yet complete" — lo shalem avon ha-Emori. Shalem is the word for whole, full, at peace — the name of Melchizedek's city two chapters ago. The delay of four hundred years is explained as waiting for something to fill up. Avon is the same word Cain used in 4:13, which means both the wrongdoing and the punishment owed for it.

chapters.title: Hagar, and the God of Seeing
chapters.html:
Genesis 16

1And Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him nothing. And she had an Egyptian servant girl, and her name was Hagar.

2And Sarai said to Abram, "Look now — the LORD has held me back from bearing. Come, please, to my servant girl. Perhaps I will be built up from her." And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.

3And Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her servant girl — at the end of ten years of Abram's dwelling in the land of Canaan — and gave her to Abram her husband, to him as a wife.

4And he came to Hagar, and she conceived. And she saw that she had conceived, and her mistress became light in her eyes.

5And Sarai said to Abram, "My violence is upon you. I myself gave my servant girl into your lap, and she saw that she had conceived, and I became light in her eyes. Let the LORD judge between me and you."

6And Abram said to Sarai, "Look — your servant girl is in your hand. Do to her what is good in your eyes." And Sarai afflicted her, and she fled from her face.

The Spring on the Way

7And the messenger of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, by the spring on the way to Shur.

8And he said, "Hagar, servant girl of Sarai, where have you come from, and where are you going?" And she said, "From the face of Sarai my mistress I am fleeing."

9And the messenger of the LORD said to her, "Return to your mistress, and submit yourself under her hands."

10And the messenger of the LORD said to her, "Multiplying, I will multiply your seed, and it shall not be counted for multitude."

11And the messenger of the LORD said to her, "Look — you are with child, and you shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Ishmael, for the LORD has heard your affliction.

12And he shall be a wild donkey of a man. His hand against all, and the hand of all against him; and in the face of all his brothers he shall dwell."

13And she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, "You are God of my seeing," for she said, "Have I even here seen after the One who sees me?"

14Therefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi — Well of the Living One who sees me. Here it is, between Kadesh and Bered.

15And Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram called the name of his son whom Hagar bore, Ishmael.

16And Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.

Notes

  • v2 "Perhaps I will be built up from her" — ulai ibbaneh mimmennah, from banah, to build — the verb used of the woman in 2:22, where God built the side into a woman. Hebrew hears ben, son, inside it: to be built is to be given a son. English can keep "built up" but cannot keep the son inside the word.

  • v2 "And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai" — va-yishma Avram le-qol Sarai. This is the sentence God spoke in 3:17, word for word in its construction: because you listened to the voice of your wife. It has not appeared in between. The book saves it for here, and it is the only comment the narrator makes on the whole arrangement.

  • v4 "her mistress became light in her eyes" — va-teqal, from qalal, to be light, slight, of no weight. It is the verb from 12:3 — the one who treats you lightly I will curse — and it has now happened inside Abram's own tent, in both directions: Hagar makes Sarai light in v4, and Sarai says I became light in her eyes in v5. The promise of 12:3 has a household problem.

  • v5 "My violence is upon you" — chamasi alekha. Chamas is the word that filled the earth before the flood in 6:11 and 6:13 — lawless seizure, the taking of what is not yours. Sarai uses the flood-word for what has been done to her, three verses after she arranged it herself.

  • v5 "between me and you" — the Masoretes placed a dot over the final letter of u-veinekha, "and you." These marks — a handful of them across the Hebrew Bible — are scribal flags on something the copyists found odd, and the tradition preserved the dot without ever explaining it or changing the text. The dot is still there, on this word, in the manuscripts we read from.

  • v6 "And Sarai afflicted her" — va-te'anneha, from anah. Fourteen verses earlier, in 15:13, God told Abram that his seed would be sojourners in a land not theirs, and that the people there would serve them and afflict them — ve-innu otam, the same verb. The word for what Egypt will do to Abram's descendants is used here for what Abram's household does to an Egyptian, in the next chapter but one. And the name Ishmael is given in v11 because the LORD has heard your affliction — onyekh, the same root a third time.

  • v6 "and she fled from her face" — va-tivrach. She is the first person in the Bible to run away.

  • v7 "the messenger of the LORD" — mal'akh YHWH, the first occurrence in the Bible. Mal'akh means a sent one, a courier; "angel" comes to English through Greek angelos, which is the same word. It is a job, not a species. And the first person he is sent to is a runaway foreign slave.

  • v8 "where have you come from, and where are you going?" — the first question anyone is asked in this book since Where are you? in 3:9 and Where is Abel your brother? in 4:9. God's questions in Genesis are addressed to people who are hiding.

  • v9 "submit yourself under her hands" — ve-hit'anni, the reflexive of the same anah that Sarai did to her in v6. She is told to go back and put herself under the thing she ran from. The text records the instruction and offers no softening of it.

  • v12 "a wild donkey of a man" — pere adam. The pere is the untamed onager of the desert, and the phrase is not obviously an insult; Job 39 describes the wild donkey as a creature that scorns the city and answers to no driver. Freedom and unmanageability in one animal.

  • v13 "she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her" — Hagar names God. No one else in the Hebrew Bible does this. Abram builds altars and calls on the name; she gives one. And she is an Egyptian slave woman, running, pregnant, with no standing in anyone's household.

  • v13 "God of my seeing… Have I even here seen after the One who sees me?" — El Ro'i, and then a sentence that has defeated everyone: ha-gam halom ra'iti acharei ro'i. The words are all common and the sense will not resolve. Has she seen and lived? Has she seen the back of the one who sees her? Is halom, "here," pointing at the place or at her survival? The verse is built entirely out of the root ra'ah, to see, four times in two lines, and the naming is certain even where the sentence is not.

chapters.title: New Names, and the Sign in the Flesh
chapters.html:
Genesis 17

1And Abram was ninety-nine years old, and the LORD appeared to Abram and said to him, "I am God Almighty. Walk about before Me, and be whole.

2And I will set My covenant between Me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly, exceedingly."

3And Abram fell on his face, and God spoke with him, saying,

4"As for Me — here is My covenant with you. And you shall become father of a roar of nations.

5And your name shall no longer be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, for father of a roar of nations I have made you.

6And I will make you fruitful exceedingly, exceedingly, and I will make you into nations, and kings shall come out of you.

7And I will raise up My covenant between Me and you, and between your seed after you through their generations, for an everlasting covenant — to be God to you, and to your seed after you.

8And I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land of your sojournings — all the land of Canaan — as an everlasting holding. And I will be God to them."

The Sign

9And God said to Abraham, "And you — you shall keep My covenant, you and your seed after you through their generations.

10This is My covenant that you shall keep, between Me and you and your seed after you: every male among you shall be circumcised.

11And you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of covenant between Me and you.

12And at eight days old every male among you shall be circumcised, through your generations — one born of the house, and one bought with silver from any foreigner who is not of your seed.

13Circumcised, he must be circumcised — the one born of your house and the one bought with your silver. And My covenant shall be in your flesh, an everlasting covenant.

14And an uncircumcised male, who does not circumcise the flesh of his foreskin — that soul shall be cut off from his people. He has broken My covenant."

Sarah

15And God said to Abraham, "Sarai your wife — you shall not call her name Sarai, for Sarah is her name.

16And I will bless her, and also give you a son from her. And I will bless her, and she shall become nations. Kings of peoples shall come from her."

17And Abraham fell on his face, and he laughed. And he said in his heart, "Shall a child be born to a man of a hundred years? And shall Sarah, a daughter of ninety years, bear?"

18And Abraham said to God, "If only Ishmael might live before You."

19And God said, "No — Sarah your wife is bearing you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac. And I will raise up My covenant with him, for an everlasting covenant, for his seed after him.

20And as for Ishmael, I have heard you. Look — I have blessed him, and I will make him fruitful, and I will multiply him exceedingly, exceedingly. Twelve chieftains he shall father, and I will make him into a great nation.

21But My covenant I will raise up with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this appointed time next year."

22And He finished speaking with him, and God went up from upon Abraham.

23And Abraham took Ishmael his son, and all born of his house, and all bought with his silver — every male among the men of Abraham's house — and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskin on the bone of that same day, as God had spoken with him.

24And Abraham was ninety-nine years old when the flesh of his foreskin was circumcised.

25And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old when the flesh of his foreskin was circumcised.

26On the bone of that same day Abraham was circumcised, and Ishmael his son.

27And all the men of his house — born of the house and bought with silver from a foreigner — were circumcised with him.

Notes

  • v1 "God Almighty" — El Shaddai, and nobody knows what Shaddai means. It has been tied to a word for mountain, to a word for breast, to a root for destroying; none of these is established. "Almighty" comes down to English through the Greek and Latin translators, who had to pick something. The name appears here for the first time in the Bible, and it is used mostly in the Abraham stories and in Job.

  • v1 "Walk about before Me, and be whole" — hithhallekh lefanai ve-heyeh tamim. Hithhallekh is the form used of God walking about in the garden (3:8), of Enoch (5:22, 24) and of Noah (6:9) — the two men who walked with God. Abraham is told to walk before Him, which is different. And tamim, whole, is the word used of Noah in 6:9: unblemished, entire, sound. It is the word for an animal fit to be offered.

  • v2, 6, 20 "exceedingly, exceedingly" — bi-me'od me'od, the intensifier doubled, three times in this chapter. It last appeared doubled in 7:19, where the flood waters overpowered exceedingly, exceedingly. The construction is rare and the book saves it.

  • vv4–5 "father of a roar of nations" — av hamon goyim. Hamon is not "multitude" in the sense of a count; it is the noise a crowd makes — a tumult, a roar, a rumble. Isaiah uses it of the sea. The promise is not that his descendants will be numerous but that they will be loud enough to hear.

  • v5 "Abram… Abraham" — the name changes by one letter, a he inserted into the middle. Av-ram is "exalted father," which is what he was called for ninety-nine years while childless. The new name is explained in the verse as av hamon, father of a roar — which is a play on the sound rather than a derivation; Abraham is not literally built from hamon. The text is doing what Lamech did with Noah in 5:29: making the name mean what the moment needs it to mean.

  • v10 "every male among you shall be circumcised" — the sign of this covenant is not a rainbow set in the sky where God will see it (9:13–16), and not animals cut in half while God passes alone through the pieces (15:17). It is cut into the people themselves, permanently, in the place the next generation comes from. The three covenant signs in this book move steadily closer in: sky, ground, body.

  • v13 "Circumcised, he must be circumcised" — the infinitive absolute doubling the verb, the same construction as mot tamut, "dying you shall die," in 2:17. It is the grammar of a decree.

  • v14 "shall be cut off" — ve-nikhretah, from karat, to cut. The same verb as karat berit, to cut a covenant (15:18). The one who will not be cut is cut off. The pun is in the Hebrew and is exact.

  • v15 "Sarai… Sarah" — her name changes too, and hers is the only woman's name changed by God in the Hebrew Bible. Both forms appear to mean princess or noblewoman; unlike Abraham's, this change is given no explanation at all. One letter, and the text moves on.

  • v17 "and he laughed" — va-yitschaq. And in v19 the son is named Yitschaq, Isaac — he laughs. The name is the father's reaction turned into a person. Abraham falls on his face in v3 in reverence and falls on his face again in v17 laughing, and God names the child after the second one.

  • v17 "Shall a child be born to a man of a hundred years?" — he says this in his heart. The laugh is silent, and God answers it in the next verse anyway. When Sarah laughs the same laugh in 18:12, also to herself, she is asked about it directly.

  • v18 "If only Ishmael might live before You" — Abraham's only request in the chapter, and it is to keep the son he already has rather than receive the one he is promised. Lu, "if only," is the particle of wishing for something you do not expect.

  • v20 "I have heard you" — shema'tikha, and the boy's name is Yishma-El, God hears. The pun is made deliberately: as for Ishmael, I have heard you. The same wordplay was made to Hagar in 16:11. Both times, the hearing is for the son who is not the chosen one.

  • v23, 26 "on the bone of that same day" — be-etsem ha-yom ha-zeh, the idiom from 7:13, where Noah entered the box. Both times it marks a day on which a thing was done without delay, the moment the word came.

  • The arithmetic — Abraham is ninety-nine, Ishmael thirteen. Ishmael was born in 16:16 when Abraham was eighty-six. Thirteen silent years pass between the two chapters, and the text says nothing about any of them.

chapters.title: Three Men at the Tent, and the Bargain
chapters.html:
Genesis 18

1And the LORD appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, and he was sitting at the opening of the tent in the heat of the day.

2And he lifted his eyes and saw, and here — three men standing over him. And he saw, and he ran to meet them from the opening of the tent, and he bowed to the ground.

3And he said, "My lord, if now I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by from over your servant.

4Let a little water be taken, and wash your feet, and lean back under the tree.

5And let me take a morsel of bread, and sustain your heart; after that you may pass on — for this is why you have passed by your servant." And they said, "So do, as you have spoken."

6And Abraham hurried to the tent, to Sarah, and said, "Hurry — three measures of fine flour! Knead it and make loaves."

7And to the herd Abraham ran, and he took a calf, tender and good, and gave it to the young man, and he hurried to make it ready.

8And he took curds and milk and the calf that he had made ready, and he set it before them. And he was standing over them under the tree, and they ate.

9And they said to him, "Where is Sarah your wife?" And he said, "Here, in the tent."

10And He said, "Returning, I will return to you at the time of life — and here, a son for Sarah your wife." And Sarah was listening at the opening of the tent, and it was behind him.

11And Abraham and Sarah were old, coming on in days. The way of women had ceased to be for Sarah.

12And Sarah laughed within herself, saying, "After I am worn out, shall I have pleasure — and my lord is old?"

13And the LORD said to Abraham, "Why is this — Sarah laughed, saying, 'Shall I truly bear, and I am old?'

14Is any word too wondrous for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, at the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son."

15And Sarah denied it, saying, "I did not laugh" — for she was afraid. And He said, "No. You did laugh."

Shall the Judge of All the Earth Not Do Justice?

16And the men rose from there and looked down over the face of Sodom. And Abraham was walking with them, to send them off.

17And the LORD said, "Shall I cover from Abraham what I am doing?

18And Abraham — becoming, he shall become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him.

19For I have known him, so that he may charge his sons and his house after him, and they shall keep the way of the LORD, to do righteousness and judgment — so that the LORD may bring upon Abraham what He has spoken concerning him."

20And the LORD said, "The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah — how great it is; and their sin — how very heavy.

21Let Me go down now and see whether they have done altogether according to her outcry that has come to Me. And if not, I will know."

22And the men turned from there and went toward Sodom. And Abraham was still standing before the LORD.

23And Abraham drew near and said, "Will You really sweep away the righteous with the wicked?

24Perhaps there are fifty righteous within the city. Will You really sweep away and not lift the place for the sake of the fifty righteous within it?

25Far be it from You to do a thing like this — to put the righteous to death with the wicked, so that the righteous should be as the wicked. Far be it from You. Shall the Judge of all the earth not do judgment?"

26And the LORD said, "If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will lift the whole place for their sake."

27And Abraham answered and said, "Look now — I have undertaken to speak to my Lord, and I am dust and ashes.

28Perhaps the fifty righteous will lack five. Will You ruin the whole city for five?" And He said, "I will not ruin, if I find there forty-five."

29And he spoke to Him yet again and said, "Perhaps forty will be found there." And He said, "I will not do it, for the sake of the forty."

30And he said, "Let it not burn in my Lord, and let me speak. Perhaps thirty will be found there." And He said, "I will not do it, if I find thirty there."

31And he said, "Look now — I have undertaken to speak to my Lord. Perhaps twenty will be found there." And He said, "I will not ruin, for the sake of the twenty."

32And he said, "Let it not burn in my Lord, and let me speak only this once. Perhaps ten will be found there." And He said, "I will not ruin, for the sake of the ten."

33And the LORD went, as He finished speaking to Abraham. And Abraham returned to his place.

Notes

  • vv1–2 "the LORD appeared to him… three men" — the chapter opens by saying the LORD appeared, and then what Abraham sees is three men. The text never reconciles the two. Through the scene the verbs slide between plural and singular: they said in v9, He said in v10, they ate in v8. The Hebrew does not explain the arithmetic and neither does this rendering.

  • vv4–8 "a little water… a morsel of bread" — and then he produces three se'ahs of fine flour, which is something over twenty liters, a whole calf, curds and milk. He offers almost nothing and delivers a feast. Hospitality in this world is understated in the offering and extravagant in the doing.

  • vv6–7 "hurried… Hurry… ran… hurried" — four verbs of haste in two verses, plus ran in v2. A ninety-nine-year-old man, three days after being circumcised, is sprinting.

  • v9 "And they said to him" — the Masoretes put a dot over every letter of the word elav, "to him," here. These marks are rare — a handful across the whole Hebrew Bible — and the scribes who made them left the text untouched and simply flagged it. What they meant by it was never written down. This is the second one in Genesis; the other is on Sarai's accusation in 16:5.

  • v10 "at the time of life" — ka-et chayyah, an idiom meaning roughly this time next year, when the season comes round living again. It is repeated in v14 and rendered literally both times because the phrase is about life returning and the chapter is about a womb.

  • v12 "shall I have pleasure" — ednah, a rare noun from the same root as Eden: delight, luxuriance. A ninety-year-old woman, laughing to herself behind a tent flap, uses the word the garden is named for.

  • vv12–13 what she said, and what God repeats — she says and my lord is old. God quotes her back to Abraham as and I am old. The words are changed in the repetition, and the change removes the part about her husband. Both verses are right here, four words apart, and any reader of the Hebrew can see the swap.

  • v14 "too wondrous" — ha-yippale, from pala, the root for what is extraordinary, surpassing, beyond reach. Not "too hard," which suggests effort. The question is whether anything lies outside the category of things the LORD does.

  • v15 — four short clauses and the chapter's whole exchange between God and Sarah: I did not laugh — for she was afraid — No. You did laugh. It is the only time she is spoken to directly, and it is a contradiction.

  • v20 "the outcry" — za'aqat. This noun is the technical word for the scream of someone being wronged — the cry that reaches a judge. It is what Abel's blood does from the ground in 4:10. Sodom is not described here by what its people do; it is described by the noise coming out of it.

  • v21 "Let Me go down now and see" — the same descent as 11:5, where the LORD came down to see the city and the tower. Both times the sentence is flat, and both times what is being looked at is a city.

  • v22 "Abraham was still standing before the LORD" — the men leave for Sodom; he does not move. The whole bargain happens in the space made by his not going.

  • v23 "sweep away" — saphah, a violent verb for gathering something up and carrying it off entirely. Not "destroy," which is the word he uses later in v28 — tashchit, the flood verb from 6:13. He starts with one word and moves to the heavier one as the count comes down.

  • v25 "Far be it from You" — chalilah lekha, twice in one verse. The phrase is close to it would be a profanation for you. He is telling God what God may not do.

  • v27 "I am dust and ashes" — aphar va-epher, two words that rhyme in Hebrew as they nearly do in English. Aphar is the dust the man was made from in 2:7 and returns to in 3:19; epher is what is left after burning. He says it in the middle of negotiating.

  • The count: 50, 45, 40, 30, 20, 10 — the steps are five, five, ten, ten, ten. He makes the first cut small, then grows bolder, then stops. Nothing in the text says why he stops at ten, and he does not ask about one.

  • v33 "And the LORD went… And Abraham returned to his place" — two clauses, no farewell, no verdict. The bargaining simply ends, and the next chapter opens in Sodom at evening.
