chapters.title: Give Me Sons, and If Not, I Am Dead
chapters.html:
Genesis 30

1And Rachel saw that she had borne Jacob no children, and Rachel was jealous of her sister. And she said to Jacob, "Give me sons — and if not, I am dead."

2And Jacob's anger burned against Rachel, and he said, "Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?"

3And she said, "Here is my maidservant Bilhah. Come to her, and let her bear upon my knees, and I too will be built up from her."

4And she gave him Bilhah her servant girl as a wife, and Jacob came to her.

5And Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.

6And Rachel said, "God has judged me, and He has also heard my voice and given me a son." Therefore she called his name Dan.

7And Bilhah, Rachel's servant girl, conceived again and bore a second son to Jacob.

8And Rachel said, "Wrestlings of God I have wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed." And she called his name Naphtali.

9And Leah saw that she had stopped bearing, and she took Zilpah her servant girl and gave her to Jacob as a wife.

10And Zilpah, Leah's servant girl, bore Jacob a son.

11And Leah said, "Fortune has come." And she called his name Gad.

12And Zilpah, Leah's servant girl, bore a second son to Jacob.

13And Leah said, "In my happiness — for the daughters will call me happy." And she called his name Asher.

The Mandrakes

14And Reuben went out in the days of the wheat harvest and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them to Leah his mother. And Rachel said to Leah, "Give me, please, some of your son's mandrakes."

15And she said to her, "Is it a small thing, your taking my husband — and you would take my son's mandrakes as well?" And Rachel said, "Then let him lie with you tonight, for your son's mandrakes."

16And Jacob came in from the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him and said, "You will come to me, for I have surely hired you with my son's mandrakes." And he lay with her that night.

17And God heard Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son.

18And Leah said, "God has given my wages, because I gave my servant girl to my husband." And she called his name Issachar.

19And Leah conceived again and bore a sixth son to Jacob.

20And Leah said, "God has endowed me with a good endowment. This time my husband will dwell with me, for I have borne him six sons." And she called his name Zebulun.

21And afterward she bore a daughter, and she called her name Dinah.

22And God remembered Rachel, and God heard her, and He opened her womb.

23And she conceived and bore a son, and she said, "God has gathered up my disgrace."

24And she called his name Joseph, saying, "May the LORD add to me another son."

Name Your Wages

25And it came to pass, when Rachel had borne Joseph, that Jacob said to Laban, "Send me away, and let me go to my own place and to my land.

26Give me my wives and my children, for whom I served you, and let me go — for you yourself know my service, how I served you."

27And Laban said to him, "If now I have found favor in your eyes — I have read the omens: the LORD has blessed me because of you."

28And he said, "Name your wages upon me, and I will give them."

29And he said to him, "You yourself know how I served you, and what your livestock became with me.

30For the little that was yours before me has broken out into a multitude, and the LORD has blessed you at my foot. And now — when shall I do something for my own house, I also?"

31And he said, "What shall I give you?" And Jacob said, "You shall give me nothing. If you will do this thing for me, I will go back, I will graze your flock, I will keep it.

32Let me pass through all your flock today, removing from it every speckled and spotted sheep, and every dark one among the lambs, and the spotted and speckled among the goats. And that shall be my wages.

33And my righteousness will answer for me on a later day, when you come over my wages before you: every one among the goats that is not speckled and spotted, and among the lambs that is not dark, it is stolen, with me."

34And Laban said, "Here — let it be according to your word."

35And on that day he removed the striped and spotted he-goats, and all the speckled and spotted she-goats, every one that had white in it, and every dark one among the lambs, and he gave them into the hand of his sons.

36And he set a distance of three days' journey between himself and Jacob. And Jacob was grazing the rest of Laban's flock.

37And Jacob took for himself fresh rods of poplar and almond and plane, and peeled white peelings in them, exposing the white that was on the rods.

38And he set the rods that he had peeled in the troughs, in the watering channels where the flocks came to drink, right in front of the flocks — and they went into heat when they came to drink.

39And the flocks went into heat at the rods, and the flocks bore striped, speckled, and spotted.

40And the lambs Jacob separated out, and he set the faces of the flock toward the striped and toward every dark one in Laban's flock. And he made himself droves of his own, and did not put them with Laban's flock.

41And it came to pass, whenever the vigorous of the flock went into heat, that Jacob would set the rods before the eyes of the flock, in the troughs, to make them heat at the rods.

42And when the flock was feeble he would not set them. So the feeble went to Laban, and the vigorous to Jacob.

43And the man broke out exceedingly, exceedingly, and he had many flocks, and maidservants and menservants, and camels and donkeys.

Notes

  • v1 "Give me sons — and if not, I am dead" — seven words in Hebrew: havah li vanim, ve-im ayin, metah anokhi. The last two are not "I will die." Metah is a participle and anokhi is the emphatic "I" — dead, I am. She is not predicting; she is describing her present condition. And she says it to Jacob, having just been told by the narrator in 29:31 who it is that opens wombs.

  • v2 "Am I in the place of God" — ha-tachat Elohim anokhi. He answers her anokhi with his own. Two people in two verses each saying I, and the argument is about which of them is not God. This is also the first time in the book that Jacob is angry — va-yichar af, his nose burned, which is what Hebrew anger does.

  • v3 "let her bear upon my knees, and I too will be built up from her" — ve-ibbaneh, from banah, to build. Ben, son, comes from the same root: in Hebrew, to get a child is to be built. The sentence is not new. Sarai said it in 16:2 — bo na el shifchati, ulai ibbaneh mimmennah, come to my servant girl, perhaps I will be built from her — the identical verb, the identical arrangement, and that one produced Ishmael, Hagar's contempt, and a woman driven into the desert twice. Rachel repeats it word for word two generations later.

    She also changes the word for Bilhah between verses. In her own mouth Bilhah is amati, my maidservant; when the narrator reports the handover in v4 she is shifchatah, her servant girl. Both are slave words. The one Rachel uses is the slightly higher of the two.

  • v6 "God has judged me" — dananni Elohim, root din: to judge, and specifically to decide a case in someone's favor. Not "God punished me" — vindicated me. She has won something. And it is Rachel who names him, not Bilhah, who bore him; the woman who gave birth does not speak in this chapter at all.

  • v8 "Wrestlings of God I have wrestled" — naftulei Elohim niftalti. The root is patal, to twist — used of a twisted cord and of crooked, devious speech. The noun naftulim occurs nowhere else in the Bible, so what the phrase weighs is genuinely open: Elohim may be doing the work Hebrew often gives it of an intensifier, mighty wrestlings, or she may mean the struggle was with God and her sister was only where it happened.

    What is not open is the last word. Gam yakholti, and I have prevailed — and in 32:29 the man at the ford tells Jacob you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed, va-tukhal, the same verb. The wrestling words differ; the prevailing word is the same. Rachel says of her sister, twenty years early, what the angel will say of her husband — and Jacob gets a new name for it while she gets a son she did not carry.

  • v11 "Fortune has come" — this verse preserves a scribal split that is visible on the page. The consonants written are בגד, one word; what is read aloud is בָּא גָד, two words, ba gad, fortune has come. The scribes kept a written form they did not pronounce and marked the reading beside it rather than correcting the text — the same conservatism that left Mehujael spelled two ways in one verse at 4:18.

    And gad is not only a common noun. Isaiah 65:11 condemns those who set a table for Gad, where the word is the name of a god of luck. Leah, in the middle of a fertility contest, names a son Luck.

  • v13 "In my happiness — for the daughters will call me happy" — be-oshri... ishsheruni banot, root ashar, to be happy, to be called fortunate. Two sons in a row named for good luck, from a woman who was hated in the previous chapter. And she says daughters will call her happy. She has no daughter yet; one arrives eight verses later and is not named for happiness or for anything else.

  • v14 "mandrakes" — duda'im. The consonants are those of dod, beloved, the word that runs through the Song of Songs on every page: the mandrake is the love-plant, a forked root vaguely shaped like a body, held to bring on conception. Then the chapter does what it does with everything: Rachel buys them and stays barren for eight more verses; Leah, who sells them, conceives that night.

  • v15 "Is it a small thing, your taking my husband" — ha-me'at qachtekh et ishi. This is the only sentence Leah is ever recorded saying to Rachel, and the only line in Genesis spoken between the two sisters. From Leah's side of chapter 29, Jacob was hers first: she was married to him, and Rachel arrived a week later.

  • v16 "I have surely hired you" — sakhor sekhartikha, the infinitive doubled for emphasis, and it is the vocabulary of wage labour, the same root Jacob and Laban use for his contract in vv28–33. Leah goes out to the field to tell her husband she has paid for him. The verb for what follows is va-yishkav immah, he lay with her — not the yada, to know, of 4:1. Jacob's night is a transaction on both ends.

  • v18 "Issachar" — natan Elohim sekhari, God has given my wages, root sakhar, the word from the verse before. And the name has an oddity you can see: it is written יִשָּׂשכָר, with two sibilants where only one is pronounced. The written form carries a letter the reading drops, and the scribes preserved it rather than tidy the spelling.

  • v20 "God has endowed me with a good endowment. This time my husband will dwell with me" — one sentence, two different roots, and the name matches the second. Zevadani... zeved tov is zabad, to bestow a gift. Yizbeleni is zabal, a rare verb whose noun zevul means an exalted dwelling — it is used of the temple. So the sixth name is explained twice over, and neither explanation is quite the name: it is a sentence about a gift wrapped around a sentence about finally being lived with. Six sons in, that is still what she is asking for.

  • v21 "And afterward she bore a daughter, and she called her name Dinah" — fifteen words of explanation for every son in this chapter, and for her, nothing. She is the only child here whose name is given without a reason, and she is the only daughter. Dinah is the feminine of Dan, from din, to judge — the root that got Rachel a whole sentence at v6 and gets Leah none here. Chapter 34 is hers, and it is about what is done to her rather than anything she says.

  • v22 "And God remembered Rachel" — va-yizkor Elohim, the verb used of Noah in the ark at 8:1 and of Abraham at 19:29. In these verses it never means God had forgotten. Zakhar is remembering as an act: the moment God moves on something owed.

  • vv23–24 "Joseph" — named twice in two verses, off two different roots. Asaf Elohim et cherpati, God has gathered up my disgrace — asaf, to gather in, to take away. Then yosef YHWH li ben acher, may the LORD add me another son — yasaf, to add. The name as spelled is the second. But her first sentence is the one that says what happened, and her second is a request made in the same breath as the answer: at the exact moment of getting what she said she would die without, she asks for one more. She gets him in 35:18, and it kills her.

  • v27 "I have read the omens" — nichashti, root nachash, the word for divination by signs. Laban says it plainly, in the middle of a compliment, and he is the man who in 31:30 will accuse Jacob of stealing his gods. The house Jacob married into keeps omens and idols, and nobody in the chapter treats this as remarkable.

  • vv35, 37 "everything Laban has is white" — the trick is built on his name. Lavan means white. In v35 Laban removes kol asher lavan bo, which reads word for word as every one that has white in it and also as every one that Laban is in. In v37 Jacob cuts rods of livneh — poplar, a tree named for its whiteness, the same three consonants — and peels petsalot levanot, white peelings, machsof ha-lavan, the exposing of the white. Four white words in three verses, aimed at a man named White. The Hebrew is doing out loud what the story is doing quietly: Jacob is stripping Laban.

  • v43 "And the man broke out exceedingly" — va-yifrots ha-ish me'od me'od. In v30 Jacob complained to Laban that the little that was yours before me has broken out into a multitude — va-yifrots la-rov, the same verb, about Laban's wealth increasing on Jacob's labour. Thirteen verses later it happens to Jacob, off Laban's flock. The chapter closes by using the accusation as the verdict.

speech.text: Genesis 30
And Rachel saw that she had borne Jacob no children, and Rachel was jealous of her sister. And she said to Jacob, "Give me sons — and if not, I am dead."
And Jacob's anger burned against Rachel, and he said, "Am I in the place of God, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?"
And she said, "Here is my maidservant Bilhah. Come to her, and let her bear upon my knees, and I too will be built up from her."
And she gave him Bilhah her servant girl as a wife, and Jacob came to her.
And Bilhah conceived and bore Jacob a son.
And Rachel said, "God has judged me, and He has also heard my voice and given me a son." Therefore she called his name Dan.
And Bilhah, Rachel's servant girl, conceived again and bore a second son to Jacob.
And Rachel said, "Wrestlings of God I have wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed." And she called his name Naphtali.
And Leah saw that she had stopped bearing, and she took Zilpah her servant girl and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
And Zilpah, Leah's servant girl, bore Jacob a son.
And Leah said, "Fortune has come." And she called his name Gad.
And Zilpah, Leah's servant girl, bore a second son to Jacob.
And Leah said, "In my happiness — for the daughters will call me happy." And she called his name Asher.
The Mandrakes
And Reuben went out in the days of the wheat harvest and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them to Leah his mother. And Rachel said to Leah, "Give me, please, some of your son's mandrakes."
And she said to her, "Is it a small thing, your taking my husband — and you would take my son's mandrakes as well?" And Rachel said, "Then let him lie with you tonight, for your son's mandrakes."
And Jacob came in from the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him and said, "You will come to me, for I have surely hired you with my son's mandrakes." And he lay with her that night.
And God heard Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son.
And Leah said, "God has given my wages, because I gave my servant girl to my husband." And she called his name Issachar.
And Leah conceived again and bore a sixth son to Jacob.
And Leah said, "God has endowed me with a good endowment. This time my husband will dwell with me, for I have borne him six sons." And she called his name Zebulun.
And afterward she bore a daughter, and she called her name Dinah.
And God remembered Rachel, and God heard her, and He opened her womb.
And she conceived and bore a son, and she said, "God has gathered up my disgrace."
And she called his name Joseph, saying, "May the LORD add to me another son."
Name Your Wages
And it came to pass, when Rachel had borne Joseph, that Jacob said to Laban, "Send me away, and let me go to my own place and to my land.
Give me my wives and my children, for whom I served you, and let me go — for you yourself know my service, how I served you."
And Laban said to him, "If now I have found favor in your eyes — I have read the omens: the LORD has blessed me because of you."
And he said, "Name your wages upon me, and I will give them."
And he said to him, "You yourself know how I served you, and what your livestock became with me.
For the little that was yours before me has broken out into a multitude, and the LORD has blessed you at my foot. And now — when shall I do something for my own house, I also?"
And he said, "What shall I give you?" And Jacob said, "You shall give me nothing. If you will do this thing for me, I will go back, I will graze your flock, I will keep it.

Let me pass through all your flock today, removing from it every speckled and spotted sheep, and every dark one among the lambs, and the spotted and speckled among the goats. And that shall be my wages.

And my righteousness will answer for me on a later day, when you come over my wages before you: every one among the goats that is not speckled and spotted, and among the lambs that is not dark, it is stolen, with me."
And Laban said, "Here — let it be according to your word."

And on that day he removed the striped and spotted he-goats, and all the speckled and spotted she-goats, every one that had white in it, and every dark one among the lambs, and he gave them into the hand of his sons.
And he set a distance of three days' journey between himself and Jacob. And Jacob was grazing the rest of Laban's flock.
And Jacob took for himself fresh rods of poplar and almond and plane, and peeled white peelings in them, exposing the white that was on the rods.
And he set the rods that he had peeled in the troughs, in the watering channels where the flocks came to drink, right in front of the flocks — and they went into heat when they came to drink.
And the flocks went into heat at the rods, and the flocks bore striped, speckled, and spotted.

And the lambs Jacob separated out, and he set the faces of the flock toward the striped and toward every dark one in Laban's flock. And he made himself droves of his own, and did not put them with Laban's flock.
And it came to pass, whenever the vigorous of the flock went into heat, that Jacob would set the rods before the eyes of the flock, in the troughs, to make them heat at the rods.
And when the flock was feeble he would not set them. So the feeble went to Laban, and the vigorous to Jacob.
And the man broke out exceedingly, exceedingly, and he had many flocks, and maidservants and menservants, and camels and donkeys.

chapters.title: The Heap of Witness
chapters.html:
Genesis 31

1And he heard the words of Laban's sons, saying, "Jacob has taken everything that was our father's, and from what was our father's he has made all this weight."

2And Jacob saw Laban's face, and here — it was not toward him as yesterday and the day before.

3And the LORD said to Jacob, "Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you."

4And Jacob sent and called Rachel and Leah to the field, to his flock.

5And he said to them, "I see your father's face, that it is not toward me as yesterday and the day before. But the God of my father has been with me.

6And you yourselves know that with all my strength I served your father.

7And your father has mocked me and changed my wages ten times over — and God did not let him do me harm.

8If he said this, 'The speckled shall be your wages,' then all the flock bore speckled; and if he said this, 'The striped shall be your wages,' then all the flock bore striped.

9So God has stripped away your father's livestock and given it to me.

10And it came to pass, at the time the flock went into heat, that I lifted my eyes and saw in a dream, and here — the he-goats mounting the flock were striped, speckled, and dappled.

11And the angel of God said to me in the dream, 'Jacob.' And I said, 'Here I am.'

12And he said, 'Lift your eyes now and see: all the he-goats mounting the flock are striped, speckled, and dappled — for I have seen everything Laban is doing to you.

13I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar, where you vowed a vow to me. Now rise, go out from this land, and return to the land of your kindred.'"

Two Daughters Answer

14And Rachel and Leah answered and said to him, "Do we still have a portion or an inheritance in our father's house?

15Are we not reckoned to him as foreigners? For he sold us, and he has also devoured, devoured our money.

16For all the wealth that God has stripped from our father — it is ours and our children's. So now, everything God has said to you, do."

17And Jacob rose and lifted his sons and his wives onto the camels.

18And he drove all his livestock and all his goods that he had gotten, the livestock of his acquiring that he had gotten in Paddan-aram, to come to Isaac his father, to the land of Canaan.

19And Laban had gone to shear his flock, and Rachel stole the household gods that were her father's.

20And Jacob stole the heart of Laban the Aramean, in not telling him that he was running.

21And he ran, he and all that was his, and he rose and crossed the River and set his face toward the hill country of Gilead.

The Search

22And it was told to Laban on the third day that Jacob had run.

23And he took his kinsmen with him and pursued after him a journey of seven days, and overtook him in the hill country of Gilead.

24And God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream by night and said to him, "Guard yourself, that you do not speak with Jacob from good to bad."

25And Laban overtook Jacob. And Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country, and Laban pitched his kinsmen in the hill country of Gilead.

26And Laban said to Jacob, "What have you done, that you stole my heart and drove my daughters off like captives of the sword?

27Why did you hide yourself to run, and steal me, and not tell me? I would have sent you off with joy and with songs, with timbrel and with lyre.

28And you did not let me kiss my sons and my daughters. Now you have acted the fool.

29My hand has the power to do you harm — but the God of your father spoke to me last night, saying, 'Guard yourself from speaking with Jacob from good to bad.'

30And now, you have gone, gone, because you longed, longed for your father's house. Why did you steal my gods?"

31And Jacob answered and said to Laban, "Because I was afraid — for I said, lest you tear your daughters away from me.

32With whomever you find your gods, he shall not live. In front of our kinsmen, identify what is mine with me and take it for yourself." And Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen them.

33And Laban went into Jacob's tent and into Leah's tent and into the tent of the two maidservants, and did not find. And he came out of Leah's tent and went into Rachel's tent.

34And Rachel had taken the household gods and put them in the camel's saddle-basket and sat on them. And Laban felt through the whole tent, and did not find.

35And she said to her father, "Let it not burn in my lord's eyes that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me." And he searched, and did not find the household gods.

Twenty Years

36And it burned in Jacob, and he quarreled with Laban. And Jacob answered and said to Laban, "What is my crime? What is my sin, that you have burned after me?

37For you have felt through all my things — what have you found of all your household things? Set it here, in front of my kinsmen and your kinsmen, and let them decide between the two of us.

38These twenty years I have been with you. Your ewes and your she-goats have not miscarried, and the rams of your flock I have not eaten.

39Torn flesh I did not bring to you — I made it good myself. From my hand you sought it, stolen by day or stolen by night.

40I was — by day the heat consumed me, and the frost by night, and my sleep fled from my eyes.

41This is twenty years for me in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flock, and you changed my wages ten times over.

42Had not the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, been mine, you would have sent me away empty now. God has seen my affliction and the labour of my palms, and He decided last night."

The Heap of Witness

43And Laban answered and said to Jacob, "The daughters are my daughters, and the sons are my sons, and the flock is my flock, and everything you see is mine. And to my daughters — what can I do for these today, or for their sons whom they have borne?

44And now, come, let us cut a covenant, I and you, and let it be a witness between me and you."

45And Jacob took a stone and raised it as a pillar.

46And Jacob said to his kinsmen, "Gather stones." And they took stones and made a heap, and they ate there on the heap.

47And Laban called it Yegar Sahaduta, and Jacob called it Galeed.

48And Laban said, "This heap is a witness between me and you today." Therefore its name was called Galeed —

49and Mizpah, because he said, "May the LORD keep watch between me and you when we are hidden from one another.

50If you afflict my daughters, and if you take wives beside my daughters — no man is with us. See, God is witness between me and you."

51And Laban said to Jacob, "Here is this heap, and here is the pillar I have set between me and you.

52This heap is witness, and the pillar is witness, that I will not cross this heap to you, and that you will not cross this heap and this pillar to me, for harm.

53The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor judge between us — the God of their father." And Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.

54And Jacob sacrificed a sacrifice in the hill country and called his kinsmen to eat bread. And they ate bread and spent the night in the hill country.

Notes

  • v1 "all this weight" — kol ha-kavod ha-zeh. Kavod is the noun English Bibles render glory, and its root kaved means heavy. Wealth is the oldest sense: what you own is what weighs. Laban's sons say Jacob took their father's substance and made it into all this kavod, and the word will still be the word for God's glory on Sinai. Weight, honour, and property are one idea in Hebrew, and English splits them into three unrelated words.

  • v2 "as yesterday and the day before" — kitmol shilshom, the standard Hebrew way of saying as it used to be. What English can't carry is how physical the sentence is around it: Jacob sees Laban's face, and the face is not toward him. Nothing is said. The whole break with Laban starts with a change of expression across a field.

  • v7 "changed my wages ten times over" — hechelif et maskurti aseret monim. Monim is a counting word, rare, and "ten" here is the round number Hebrew uses for repeatedly rather than a tally. The verb before it is hetel bi, from talal, to trifle with, to make a fool of — Laban did not merely underpay him, he played with him.

  • vv9, 16 "stripped away" — va-yatsel, the hiphil of natsal, to snatch out, rescue, tear away. It is the word for a lamb pulled from a lion's mouth and the word for God delivering Israel from Egypt. Jacob uses it of the flocks, and then his wives repeat it back to him in v16 about their father's wealth. In the mouths of all three, God's rescuing is what happened to Laban's property.

  • v13 "I am the God of Bethel" — anokhi ha-El Beit-El, awkward in Hebrew: I am the God, Bethel, the place-name sitting where a description should be. And Beit-El is itself house of God, so the sentence stutters — I am the God of God's-house. The angel is reaching twenty years back to 28:18, to the stone Jacob anointed on the night he left with nothing, and answering the vow Jacob made there by quoting it.

  • vv14–16 the only time they speak together — va-ta'an Rachel ve-Leah, one verb, and the two sisters who have been set against each other for three chapters say the same thing. Their case is a property case: a bride-price was normally paid to the father and held for the daughter, and Jacob paid his in fourteen years of labour. He sold us, and he has also devoured, devoured our money — akhal gam akhol, eaten and eaten. They say they were reckoned as foreigners, nokhriyyot, the word for an outsider woman with no claim in the house. They are not choosing their husband over their father. They are telling him there is nothing left to stay for.

  • vv19, 20, 26, 27, 30, 32 "stole" — ganav, six times in the chapter, and this is the spine of it. Rachel steals the household gods (19). Jacob steals Laban's heart (20) — ganav et lev, an idiom for taking someone in, deceiving; English has no verb for it. Laban accuses Jacob of stealing his heart (26) and then of stealing him (27), and finally asks why did you steal my gods (30). Jacob, who does not know, pronounces death on the thief (32). Then in v39 he uses the word for the sixth time about animals stolen from his watch, which he paid for out of his own pocket. One root carries the deception, the theft, the curse, and the twenty years of honest loss.

  • v19 "household gods" — terafim. The word is never explained in the Bible and its etymology is not recoverable; what can be said is what the text shows. They are portable, they fit under a saddle, they belong to a household, and Laban calls them elohai, my gods (v30). This is Abraham's brother's family, the people Rebekah and Rachel and Leah came from, and they keep gods in the house and read omens (30:27).

  • v24 "from good to bad" — mi-tov ad ra, an idiom that means anything whatever: God tells Laban not to say a word to Jacob, good or bad. Laban obeys the letter of it by repeating the warning back to Jacob in v29 while delivering a speech of some length. He tells Jacob he has the power to hurt him, and then explains why he isn't going to.

  • vv34–35 what Laban does not find — va-yemashesh Laban et kol ha-ohel, he felt through the whole tent, a groping, hands-on search. The gods of his house are under his daughter, who is sitting on a camel's saddle-basket claiming derekh nashim li, the way of women is upon me. In the purity terms this family lived by, that puts the household gods under the one thing that would make them unclean, and the text reports it in a flat sentence and moves on. The only comment it allows itself is the repetition: and did not find three times in three verses.

  • v32 "he shall not live" — Jacob says it in confidence, in front of witnesses, and the narrator immediately tells us he was wrong about who took them. Rachel dies in childbirth on the road in 35:19, four chapters later. The text never connects the two sentences. It only puts them in the same book, and leaves the reader to notice that the man who cursed the thief was married to her.

  • v36 "it burned" — va-yichar le-Ya'aqov. The same verb that opened 30:2, va-yichar af Ya'aqov, his anger burned at Rachel, and the same verb Rachel uses to her father in v35, al yichar, let it not burn. Jacob is angry twice in his whole story, and both times in these two chapters: once at his wife for asking him for children, and once here, at the man who took twenty years from him. It is the longest speech he makes in Genesis.

  • vv38–40 the shepherd's defence — this is a legal brief, in the technical vocabulary of herding contracts. Terefah, torn flesh, is the standing excuse of a hired shepherd: an animal killed by a predator was the owner's loss, not the herdsman's, provided the carcass was produced. Jacob says he never once used it — anokhi achattenna, from chata, the ordinary verb to sin, here in the sense of make good the shortfall, to bear the loss yourself. He absorbed the predators, the thefts by day, the thefts by night, the heat, the frost, and the sleeplessness, and he says so item by item like a man reading an invoice.

  • v42 "the Fear of Isaac" — pachad Yitzchaq, a title for God that occurs here and in v53 and nowhere else. Pachad is ordinary Hebrew for dread. What it means as a divine name is not settled and the word does not settle it: it may be the One Isaac fears, or the fear-inspiring God of Isaac. Whatever it is, Jacob deliberately does not name his God the way Laban has just named his, and in v53 the distinction is the whole point.

  • v47 the only Aramaic in Genesis — Laban names the heap Yegar Sahaduta; Jacob names it Gal-ed. The two phrases mean the same thing — heap of witness — in two different languages, and Laban's two words are the only Aramaic in the book. The narrator has been calling him Laban the Aramean since v20. This verse is where the family splits in two on the page: the branch that stayed in the north speaks Aramaic, and the branch going to Canaan speaks Hebrew, and the last thing they do together is give one pile of rocks two names.

  • v49 "Mizpah" — ha-mitspah, from tsafah, to keep watch, and the sentence that explains it is yitsef YHWH beini u-veinekha, may the LORD keep watch between me and you when we are hidden from one another. This line is printed on rings and read at weddings as a blessing for people who miss each other. In the chapter it is a surveillance clause. Two men who have just finished accusing each other of theft are agreeing that since neither will be able to see what the other does, God will have to watch — and the next verse spells out what he is watching for.

  • v53 "the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor judge between us" — yishpetu, a plural verb, which in Hebrew is what you use when the subject is more than one. Laban names two gods, one for each grandfather, and lets the verb agree with two. Then Jacob swears — and does not swear by that pair. He swears by the Fear of his father Isaac, one God, his own line only. The covenant is sealed by two men taking two different oaths on the same heap of stones.

speech.text: Genesis 31
And he heard the words of Laban's sons, saying, "Jacob has taken everything that was our father's, and from what was our father's he has made all this weight."
And Jacob saw Laban's face, and here — it was not toward him as yesterday and the day before.
And the LORD said to Jacob, "Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you."
And Jacob sent and called Rachel and Leah to the field, to his flock.
And he said to them, "I see your father's face, that it is not toward me as yesterday and the day before. But the God of my father has been with me.
And you yourselves know that with all my strength I served your father.
And your father has mocked me and changed my wages ten times over — and God did not let him do me harm.
If he said this, 'The speckled shall be your wages,' then all the flock bore speckled; and if he said this, 'The striped shall be your wages,' then all the flock bore striped.
So God has stripped away your father's livestock and given it to me.
And it came to pass, at the time the flock went into heat, that I lifted my eyes and saw in a dream, and here — the he-goats mounting the flock were striped, speckled, and dappled.
And the angel of God said to me in the dream, 'Jacob.' And I said, 'Here I am.'
And he said, 'Lift your eyes now and see: all the he-goats mounting the flock are striped, speckled, and dappled — for I have seen everything Laban is doing to you.
I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar, where you vowed a vow to me. Now rise, go out from this land, and return to the land of your kindred.'"
Two Daughters Answer
And Rachel and Leah answered and said to him, "Do we still have a portion or an inheritance in our father's house?
Are we not reckoned to him as foreigners? For he sold us, and he has also devoured, devoured our money.
For all the wealth that God has stripped from our father — it is ours and our children's. So now, everything God has said to you, do."
And Jacob rose and lifted his sons and his wives onto the camels.
And he drove all his livestock and all his goods that he had gotten, the livestock of his acquiring that he had gotten in Paddan-aram, to come to Isaac his father, to the land of Canaan.
And Laban had gone to shear his flock, and Rachel stole the household gods that were her father's.
And Jacob stole the heart of Laban the Aramean, in not telling him that he was running.
And he ran, he and all that was his, and he rose and crossed the River and set his face toward the hill country of Gilead.
The Search
And it was told to Laban on the third day that Jacob had run.
And he took his kinsmen with him and pursued after him a journey of seven days, and overtook him in the hill country of Gilead.
And God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream by night and said to him, "Guard yourself, that you do not speak with Jacob from good to bad."
And Laban overtook Jacob. And Jacob had pitched his tent in the hill country, and Laban pitched his kinsmen in the hill country of Gilead.
And Laban said to Jacob, "What have you done, that you stole my heart and drove my daughters off like captives of the sword?
Why did you hide yourself to run, and steal me, and not tell me? I would have sent you off with joy and with songs, with timbrel and with lyre.
And you did not let me kiss my sons and my daughters. Now you have acted the fool.
My hand has the power to do you harm — but the God of your father spoke to me last night, saying, 'Guard yourself from speaking with Jacob from good to bad.'
And now, you have gone, gone, because you longed, longed for your father's house. Why did you steal my gods?"
And Jacob answered and said to Laban, "Because I was afraid — for I said, lest you tear your daughters away from me.
With whomever you find your gods, he shall not live. In front of our kinsmen, identify what is mine with me and take it for yourself." And Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen them.
And Laban went into Jacob's tent and into Leah's tent and into the tent of the two maidservants, and did not find. And he came out of Leah's tent and went into Rachel's tent.
And Rachel had taken the household gods and put them in the camel's saddle-basket and sat on them. And Laban felt through the whole tent, and did not find.
And she said to her father, "Let it not burn in my lord's eyes that I cannot rise before you, for the way of women is upon me." And he searched, and did not find the household gods.
Twenty Years
And it burned in Jacob, and he quarreled with Laban. And Jacob answered and said to Laban, "What is my crime? What is my sin, that you have burned after me?
For you have felt through all my things — what have you found of all your household things? Set it here, in front of my kinsmen and your kinsmen, and let them decide between the two of us.
These twenty years I have been with you. Your ewes and your she-goats have not miscarried, and the rams of your flock I have not eaten.
Torn flesh I did not bring to you — I made it good myself. From my hand you sought it, stolen by day or stolen by night.
I was — by day the heat consumed me, and the frost by night, and my sleep fled from my eyes.
This is twenty years for me in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flock, and you changed my wages ten times over.

Had not the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, been mine, you would have sent me away empty now. God has seen my affliction and the labour of my palms, and He decided last night."
The Heap of Witness

And Laban answered and said to Jacob, "The daughters are my daughters, and the sons are my sons, and the flock is my flock, and everything you see is mine. And to my daughters — what can I do for these today, or for their sons whom they have borne?
And now, come, let us cut a covenant, I and you, and let it be a witness between me and you."
And Jacob took a stone and raised it as a pillar.
And Jacob said to his kinsmen, "Gather stones." And they took stones and made a heap, and they ate there on the heap.
And Laban called it Yegar Sahaduta, and Jacob called it Galeed.
And Laban said, "This heap is a witness between me and you today." Therefore its name was called Galeed —
and Mizpah, because he said, "May the LORD keep watch between me and you when we are hidden from one another.
If you afflict my daughters, and if you take wives beside my daughters — no man is with us. See, God is witness between me and you."
And Laban said to Jacob, "Here is this heap, and here is the pillar I have set between me and you.
This heap is witness, and the pillar is witness, that I will not cross this heap to you, and that you will not cross this heap and this pillar to me, for harm.
The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor judge between us — the God of their father." And Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.
And Jacob sacrificed a sacrifice in the hill country and called his kinsmen to eat bread. And they ate bread and spent the night in the hill country.

chapters.title: A Man Wrestled With Him Until the Dawn Came Up
chapters.html:
Genesis 32

1And Laban rose early in the morning and kissed his sons and his daughters and blessed them. And Laban went, and returned to his place.

2And Jacob went on his way, and the messengers of God met him.

3And Jacob said when he saw them, "This is God's camp." And he called the name of that place Mahanaim.

Four Hundred Men

4And Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to Esau his brother, to the land of Seir, the field of Edom.

5And he commanded them, saying, "So shall you say to my lord, to Esau: 'So says your servant Jacob: I have sojourned with Laban and stayed until now.

6And I have come to have ox and donkey, flock and manservant and maidservant. And I have sent to tell my lord, to find favor in your eyes.'"

7And the messengers returned to Jacob, saying, "We came to your brother, to Esau — and he is also coming to meet you, and four hundred men with him."

8And Jacob was very afraid, and it was narrow for him. And he divided the people who were with him, and the flocks and the herds and the camels, into two camps.

9And he said, "If Esau comes to the one camp and strikes it, then the camp that is left will be an escape."

10And Jacob said, "God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, LORD who said to me, 'Return to your land and to your kindred, and I will do well by you' —

11I am too small for all the kindnesses and all the faithfulness you have done for your servant. For with my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps.

12Deliver me, please, from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau — for I am afraid of him, lest he come and strike me, mother upon sons.

13And you yourself said, 'I will surely do well by you, and I will make your seed like the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted for multitude.'"

14And he spent the night there that night. And he took from what had come into his hand a gift for Esau his brother:

15two hundred she-goats and twenty he-goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams,

16thirty nursing camels and their young, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty she-donkeys and ten young donkeys.

17And he gave them into the hand of his servants, drove by drove on its own, and said to his servants, "Cross over ahead of me, and put a space between drove and drove."

18And he commanded the first, saying, "When Esau my brother meets you and asks you, saying, 'Whose are you, and where are you going, and whose are these ahead of you?' —

19then you shall say, 'Your servant Jacob's. It is a gift sent to my lord, to Esau. And here — he is also behind us.'"

20And he commanded the second also, and the third also, and all those going behind the droves also, saying, "In this manner you shall speak to Esau when you find him.

21And you shall say also, 'Here — your servant Jacob is behind us.'" For he said, "Let me cover his face with the gift that goes ahead of me, and afterward I will see his face. Perhaps he will lift my face."

22And the gift crossed over ahead of his face, and he spent that night in the camp.

The Ford of the Jabbok

23And he rose that night and took his two wives and his two servant girls and his eleven children, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok.

24And he took them and brought them across the stream, and he brought across what was his.

25And Jacob was left alone. And a man wrestled with him until the dawn came up.

26And he saw that he could not prevail against him, and he touched the socket of his thigh, and the socket of Jacob's thigh was wrenched as he wrestled with him.

27And he said, "Send me away, for the dawn has come up." And he said, "I will not send you away unless you bless me."

28And he said to him, "What is your name?" And he said, "Jacob."

29And he said, "Your name shall no longer be said as Jacob, but Israel — for you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed."

30And Jacob asked and said, "Tell me, please, your name." And he said, "Why is this that you ask for my name?" And he blessed him there.

31And Jacob called the name of the place Peniel — "for I have seen God face to face, and my life was delivered."

32And the sun rose upon him as he crossed Penuel, and he was limping on his thigh.

33Therefore the sons of Israel do not eat the sinew of the hip that is on the socket of the thigh, to this day, because he touched the socket of Jacob's thigh, at the sinew of the hip.

Notes

  • On the verse numbers in this chapter — the Hebrew text this rendering follows begins chapter 32 with Laban's departure, so it has 33 verses. Most English Bibles put that verse at the end of chapter 31 and number this chapter 1–32. So from v1 on, every verse here is one higher than the same words in an NIV or ESV: the wrestling match is 32:25–33 here and 32:24–32 there. Chapter 33 lines up again.

  • v2 "the messengers of God met him" — va-yifge'u vo mal'akhei Elohim, and the verb is the one from 28:11, where Jacob leaving home va-yifga ba-maqom, met the place, and slept there, and saw the ladder. Paga is not a gentle word for meeting; it means to run into, to come up against, and in other contexts to fall upon someone. Twenty years ago it happened to him on the way out and there were angels on a ladder. Now it happens on the way back, in a single sentence, with no explanation of what they wanted.

  • vv2, 4 "messengers" — Hebrew has one word, mal'akh, for a messenger and for what English calls an angel. God's mal'akhim meet Jacob in v2; Jacob sends his own mal'akhim to Esau in v4. The same word, back to back, and English cannot do it — the moment you write "angels" in one verse and "messengers" in the next, the echo is gone.

  • v3 "Mahanaim" — machanayim, and the ending is Hebrew's dual, a grammatical number for things that come in twos, used for eyes, ears, hands. The name means two camps. Five verses later, afraid, Jacob splits everything he owns into shnei machanot, two camps, and in v11 he prays I have become two camps. He names the place before he knows why, and the rest of the chapter is spent earning the name.

  • v6 "ox and donkey, flock and manservant and maidservant" — every noun singular, a short and modest list from a man the previous chapter left with flocks, servants, camels and donkeys in quantity (30:43). The camels are missing. He is about to send Esau a gift of five hundred and fifty head, and the message he sends first understates what he has.

  • v8 "it was narrow for him" — va-yetser lo, from tsarar, to be tight, to press in. Hebrew distress is spatial: the walls come in. English "distress" is from the same picture — Latin stringere, to draw tight — but nobody feels it any more, and the Hebrew is still literal.

  • v11 "I am too small" — qatonti. One word, a verb, and no English equivalent is one word: I have been made small by, I am less than. Not modesty; a measurement. And then with my staff I crossed this Jordan — be-maqli, and maqel is the same word as the peeled rods of 30:37, the trick that made him rich. He came across the river owning one stick. He is going back across with two camps, and the word for the stick is the word for the con.

  • v11 "kindnesses... faithfulness" — chasadim and emet, the pair that runs through the rest of the Bible as chesed ve-emet. Chesed is loyalty inside a relationship — not generosity to a stranger but keeping faith with your own; emet is from aman, to be firm, which is also where amen comes from. Together they mean something like the loyalty that holds and does not shift, and Jacob is saying he does not measure up to the amount of it he has received.

  • v12 "mother upon sons" — em al banim, a set phrase for annihilation: not the fighters killed and the household taken, but the whole line ended in one place. Jacob, who has just spent two chapters counting livestock, prays about his children.

  • vv21–22 "face" — panim, five times in two verses, and it is the hinge of the chapter. Akhapperah fanav — let me cover his face with the gift. Ve-acharei khen er'eh fanav — afterward I will see his face. Ulai yissa fanai — perhaps he will lift my face, the idiom for accepting a person, showing favor. Va-ta'avor ha-minchah al panav — the gift crossed over ahead of his face.

    And the verb in the first of them is kaphar, which means to cover, and which is the verb the whole sacrificial system is built on — the Day of Kippur is the day of covering. Its first appearance in this sense in the Bible is here, and it is not a priest and an altar. It is a frightened man sending goats ahead of him to cover his brother's face before he has to look at it.

    Ten verses later he names a place Peniel, face of God, and says I have seen God face to face. The chapter spends its whole length on one word.

  • v23 "the ford of the Jabbok" — ma'avar Yabboq, and three words in this chapter are built from nearly the same three letters. Yabboq, the river. Ya'aqov, Jacob. Ye'aveq, he wrestled. Y-b-q, y-'-q-b, '-b-q — the place, the man, and the act, turning over each other like the letters themselves. It is the densest piece of wordplay in Genesis, and no English rendering can show it without stopping to explain, which is what this note is for.

  • v25 "a man wrestled with him" — ish, a man. Not an angel, not the LORD, not a stranger: the plainest word in the language for an adult male. The text says nothing else about him for six verses, refuses to give his name when asked, and lets Jacob be the one to conclude in v31 that he has seen God. Every reading that arrives faster than that is arriving faster than the text.

  • v26 "the socket of his thigh" — kaf yerekh, the hollow or cup of the hip. Yerekh is also the euphemism for the loins as the source of offspring — Genesis 46:26 counts the people who came out of Jacob's yerekh. The man cannot beat him, so he touches him once, and the place he touches is where the sons come from, on the night before Jacob meets the brother who wanted to kill him and after the eleventh son is born.

  • v27 "Send me away" — shallecheni, the exact word Jacob said to Laban in 30:25: send me away, and let me go to my own place. Jacob spent twenty years asking to be let go. He now has hold of someone who is asking him for it, and he says no.

  • vv28–29 "What is your name?" — the last time Jacob was asked who he was, it was his blind father in 27:18, mi attah beni, who are you, my son — and he answered I am Esau your firstborn, and stole the blessing with the lie. Here he is asked again, in the dark, on the night he has to face the brother he stole it from. This time he says Jacob, which is the name that means heel-grabber and supplanter, and which Esau in 27:36 turned into a complaint — is he not rightly named Jacob, for he has supplanted me twice. He gives his real name and gets the blessing anyway, and a new name with it.

  • v29 "Israel" — ki sarita im Elohim ve-im anashim va-tukhal, you have struggled with God and with men and you have prevailed. The verb is sarah, to contend, to persist — a rare root, and the name Yisra'el is built from it plus El. Two honest things. First, the name as a piece of grammar would more naturally mean God contends or God rules, since in the ordinary run of Hebrew names ending in -el — Daniel, Ishmael, Ezekiel — God is the one doing the verb. The verse assigns the verb to Jacob instead, which is either the narrator telling us what it means or a name being read against its grammar; the text does not say which. Second, va-tukhal, and you prevailed, is the word Rachel used at 30:8 about beating her sister, and the word used at v26 of this chapter for what the man could not do to Jacob. The name is given for the one thing about Jacob that never changes.

  • v30 "Why is this that you ask for my name?" — the question is refused, and the blessing is given anyway, and the man leaves before the sun is up. Jacob names the place after what he concludes happened; the story never confirms it.

  • v31 "my life was delivered" — va-tinnatsel nafshi, the verb natsal for the third time in two chapters: God stripped away Laban's flocks (31:9, 31:16), Jacob prayed deliver me from the hand of my brother (v12), and now he says his own life was pulled out. The prayer is answered in the wrong fight, before he has met Esau at all.

  • v31, 32 "Peniel... Penuel" — the place is spelled two ways in two consecutive verses, and the text leaves both, the same way it left Mehujael spelled twice at 4:18 and the written and read forms of Gad at 30:11.

  • v32 "the sun rose upon him" — va-yizrach lo ha-shemesh. When he left home in 28:11 he stopped for the night ki va ha-shemesh, because the sun had gone in, and dreamed the ladder. The sun set on him going out and rises on him coming back, and the verb is zarach, the same word used of dawn all through the Bible. Between the two sentences is everything that happened to him, and he comes back into the light limping.

  • v33 "the sinew of the hip" — gid ha-nasheh. Gid is a sinew or tendon; nasheh occurs in the Bible only in this verse, twice, so what exactly it names is not recoverable from the language — it is defined only by where it sits, on the socket of the thigh. This is the one dietary law in Genesis, it is given without a command attached, and it is explained as a memorial rather than ordered: the sons of Israel do not eat it, not shall not. The whole nation's kitchens keep the record of one night's limp.

chapters.title: As One Sees the Face of God
chapters.html:
Genesis 33

1And Jacob lifted his eyes and looked, and here — Esau coming, and four hundred men with him. And he divided the children between Leah and Rachel and the two servant girls.

2And he put the servant girls and their children first, and Leah and her children after them, and Rachel and Joseph last.

3And he himself crossed over ahead of them and bowed to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.

4And Esau ran to meet him and embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept.

5And he lifted his eyes and saw the women and the children, and said, "Who are these to you?" And he said, "The children with whom God has favored your servant."

6And the servant girls came near, they and their children, and bowed down.

7And Leah also came near, and her children, and they bowed down. And afterward Joseph came near, and Rachel, and they bowed down.

8And he said, "What to you is all this camp that I met?" And he said, "To find favor in the eyes of my lord."

9And Esau said, "I have much, my brother. Let what is yours be yours."

10And Jacob said, "No, please — if I have found favor in your eyes, then take my gift from my hand. For this is why I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God, and you have received me.

11Take, please, my blessing that has been brought to you — for God has favored me, and because I have everything." And he pressed him, and he took it.

Not to Seir

12And he said, "Let us pull up and go, and I will go alongside you."

13And he said to him, "My lord knows that the children are tender, and the flocks and the herds are nursing upon me. If they are driven hard one day, all the flock will die.

14Let my lord cross over ahead of his servant, and I will lead on at my own slowness, at the pace of the property that is before me and at the pace of the children, until I come to my lord at Seir."

15And Esau said, "Let me set with you some of the people who are with me." And he said, "Why this? Let me find favor in the eyes of my lord."

16And Esau returned that day on his way to Seir.

17And Jacob pulled up to Succoth and built himself a house, and for his livestock he made booths. Therefore he called the name of the place Succoth.

18And Jacob came whole to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, on his coming from Paddan-aram. And he camped before the face of the city.

19And he bought the portion of the field where he had pitched his tent from the hand of the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem, for a hundred qesitah.

20And he set up an altar there and called it El, God of Israel.

Notes

  • v2 the order of the line — servant girls and their children first, Leah and hers second, Rachel and Joseph last. He is arranging his family in the order he can afford to lose them, and the text says so without saying so: it gives the order, and nothing else. This is the same man who split his herds into two camps in the previous chapter so that the camp that is left will be an escape. Bilhah and Zilpah's four sons are the front rank.

  • v3 "bowed to the ground seven times" — va-yishtachu artsah sheva pe'amim, the full prostration, repeated, which is the protocol for approaching a king. And the verb is the one from his father's blessing: in 27:29 Isaac told Jacob be lord over your brothers, and let your mother's sons bow down to you — ve-yishtachavu lekha — the same verb, shachah. He got that blessing by pretending to be Esau. The first thing he does on meeting him is perform its exact reverse, seven times.

    He keeps it up all chapter. He calls Esau adoni, my lord, five times, and himself avdekha, your servant. The blessing said the brothers would serve him. He spends twenty verses saying the opposite out loud.

  • v4 "and kissed him" — this word carries a mark you can see on the page. In the Hebrew manuscripts va-yishaqehu has a dot written over every one of its letters. There are a handful of such places in the Hebrew Bible, and they are one of the oldest surviving scribal signals in the text — the scribes copied the word and flagged it, and then copied the flags for two thousand years.

    What the flag means is not written down anywhere in the text. Later readers have argued both directions, that the kiss was wholehearted and that it was not, and the dots do not settle it. What can be said with certainty is that at this word, and not at the embrace or the falling on the neck or the weeping that surround it, somebody very early had something to mark, and every copy since has kept the marking without explaining it.

  • v5 "Who are these to you?" — mi elleh lakh. Jacob has now been asked who he is in three consecutive scenes: who are you, my son by his blind father in 27:18, what is your name by the man at the ford in 32:28, and now this. The first time he lied. The second time he told the truth and was renamed. This time the question is about his children, and he answers by naming God: the children with whom God has favored your servant — chanan, to show unearned favor, the root behind the name Hannah and behind Yochanan, which becomes John.

  • vv9, 11 "much" against "everything" — Esau says yesh li rav, I have much. Jacob says yesh li khol, I have everything. One word apart, and they are the two brothers in miniature: the one who has enough and the one who cannot say enough. Jacob is the one who left with a stick.

  • v10 "as one sees the face of God" — kir'ot pnei Elohim, and the sentence is deliberate. He named a place Peniel, face of God, the night before, because I have seen God face to face and my life was delivered (32:31). Now he looks at his brother and uses the same words. Va-tirtseni, and you have received me — ratsah is the verb used of God accepting a sacrifice as acceptable. He is telling Esau that surviving him and surviving God were the same experience.

  • v11 "my blessing" — birkhati, and this is the chapter's hinge. Every earlier verse called the drove a minchah, a gift or tribute (32:14, 32:19, 33:10). Here Jacob changes the word. Berakhah is the thing he took from Esau in chapter 27 by dressing in goatskins — and what he is handing over is two hundred goats, two hundred ewes, camels, cattle and donkeys. He gives the blessing back, in the form of livestock, using its own name. And the verb is hubat lakh, brought to you, a passive with no agent, as though nobody were doing it.

    Then va-yiftsar bo va-yiqqach — he pressed him, and he took it. Three words. Esau does not want it and accepts it anyway, and the transaction that has driven the whole story since chapter 25 closes in half a verse.

  • v13 "nursing upon me" — alot alai. The flocks are giving milk and the young are on them, so the herd moves at the speed of the slowest animal. It is a true reason and a convenient one.

  • v14 "at my own slowness" — le-itti, from a root meaning gentleness or slowness, a rare word. And twice in one sentence le-regel, at the foot of — at the pace of the property, at the pace of the children. Jacob is explaining, carefully and at length, why he cannot travel with his brother.

  • vv14, 16, 17 Seir and Succoth — he says until I come to my lord at Seir. Esau leaves for Seir. Jacob goes to Succoth, in the other direction, and builds a house. The narrator sets the three sentences side by side and adds nothing. There is no rebuke, no explanation, and no later scene in which he arrives at Seir. It is simply what he said and what he did, reported in the same flat voice as the herds and the tents.

  • v17 "Succoth" — sukkot, booths or shelters: brush-and-branch structures, temporary by definition. He builds himself a bayit, a house, the first time in the book anybody builds one for himself, and makes sukkot for the cattle — and names the place after the cattle shelters rather than the house. This is the word behind the Festival of Booths, the week Israel spends living in shelters to remember having no house.

  • v18 "came whole" — va-yavo Ya'aqov shalem, and shalem is the adjective from shalom: whole, intact, unharmed, at peace, nothing missing. It can also be read as a place name. If it is the adjective, and that is the natural reading, it is the verdict on everything since he ran from Esau with nothing: twenty years with Laban, the flight, the pursuit, the night at the ford, the four hundred men — and he arrives whole, limping, but with nothing missing. The last line of the Jacob-and-Esau story is one word.

  • v18 "before the face of the city" — va-yichan et pnei ha-ir. Panim once more, the word chapter 32 was built on, and now it is a city's face he camps in front of. The city is Shechem, and chapter 34 happens there.

  • v19 "a hundred qesitah" — qesitah is a unit of money that appears three times in the entire Hebrew Bible and is never defined; nothing in the language fixes its value, and it is not used again after the oldest layers of the text. What the verse establishes is not the price but the fact: Jacob buys his ground, from named sellers, like Abraham buying the cave in chapter 23. The two purchases are the only land in Canaan the family owns.

  • v20 "El, God of Israel" — El Elohei Yisra'el. He names the altar for the name he was given at the ford, and it is the first time Israel is used for anything beyond the man himself: not my God but the God of Israel, the form the whole nation will use. Twenty-four hours after being renamed in the dark by someone who would not give a name in return, he builds a stone thing and puts the new name on it.

speech.text: Genesis 33
And Jacob lifted his eyes and looked, and here — Esau coming, and four hundred men with him. And he divided the children between Leah and Rachel and the two servant girls.
And he put the servant girls and their children first, and Leah and her children after them, and Rachel and Joseph last.
And he himself crossed over ahead of them and bowed to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.
And Esau ran to meet him and embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept.
And he lifted his eyes and saw the women and the children, and said, "Who are these to you?" And he said, "The children with whom God has favored your servant."
And the servant girls came near, they and their children, and bowed down.
And Leah also came near, and her children, and they bowed down. And afterward Joseph came near, and Rachel, and they bowed down.
And he said, "What to you is all this camp that I met?" And he said, "To find favor in the eyes of my lord."
And Esau said, "I have much, my brother. Let what is yours be yours."
And Jacob said, "No, please — if I have found favor in your eyes, then take my gift from my hand. For this is why I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God, and you have received me.
Take, please, my blessing that has been brought to you — for God has favored me, and because I have everything." And he pressed him, and he took it.
Not to Seir
And he said, "Let us pull up and go, and I will go alongside you."
And he said to him, "My lord knows that the children are tender, and the flocks and the herds are nursing upon me. If they are driven hard one day, all the flock will die.
Let my lord cross over ahead of his servant, and I will lead on at my own slowness, at the pace of the property that is before me and at the pace of the children, until I come to my lord at Seir."
And Esau said, "Let me set with you some of the people who are with me." And he said, "Why this? Let me find favor in the eyes of my lord."
And Esau returned that day on his way to Seir.
And Jacob pulled up to Succoth and built himself a house, and for his livestock he made booths. Therefore he called the name of the place Succoth.
And Jacob came whole to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, on his coming from Paddan-aram. And he camped before the face of the city.
And he bought the portion of the field where he had pitched his tent from the hand of the sons of Hamor, father of Shechem, for a hundred qesitah.
And he set up an altar there and called it El, God of Israel.
